i'm not going to let you get away with this. in taking part in this debate on the own-initiative report on the union's procedure for granting marketing authorisations for pesticides, it is worth noting that the european commission's consent to the use of glyphosate in the union, given in december 2017 for a further five years, until 2022, has caused a great deal of public discontent and has consequently led to the establishment of a special pest committee by parliament. the negative public sentiment in this case is mainly due to the august 2018 ruling of a court in the united states, which found that monsanto's glyphosate caused lymphoma in an american gardener, and awarded him nearly $300 million. the pest ad hoc committee set up by parliament in its report proposed, inter alia, greater transparency in pesticide research and the avoidance of conflicts of interest in pesticide research, as well as a ban on the use of plant protection products in public places. unfortunately, this report is not a breakthrough on the use of pesticides in agriculture.
in writing. in december 2017, the licence for the controversial herbicide containing glyphosate was renewed and allowed to be used in the eu for five years. this is a shorter period than usual (10 years), but it still worries me, especially in the context of the court's judgment delivered in san francisco on 11 august 2018. the court found that 46-year-old gardener dewayne johnson, who had used roundup for years, developed cancer of the lymphatic system from exposure to glyphosate. the court ruled that monsanto (acquired in july 2018 by the german pharmaceutical group bayer) deliberately concealed the harmfulness of the substance and must now pay nearly $290 million in compensation to a gardener who doctors say has two years left to live. the verdict points to overwhelming evidence of the harmfulness of glyphosate. germany's bayer intends to appeal the decision. if this judgment is upheld, however, it could set a precedent for a wave of similar decisions. i believe that the continued release of glyphosate is not only controversial, but above all dangerous to human health and life. this is a matter of widespread public concern and therefore new, comprehensive analyses and evaluations of this product must be carried out continuously. active substances for which it cannot be demonstrated that the strict approval criteria provided for in the legislation are met should be withdrawn from the market on a continuous basis.

in writing. the report on the use of driverless hire vehicles for the carriage of goods by road is an important step towards the realisation of the idea and principles of a single transport market. it will allow individual businesses to lease and operate fleets of vehicles across the eu for up to four months, allowing them greater regulatory flexibility and the ability to respond on an ongoing basis to, for example, seasonal market needs. until now, member states have been free to introduce any rules they wish to restrict such practices, which has forced companies to use their own fleets. the new legal framework will also give us more control over air quality, as the chartered fleet will have to meet high environmental standards to be allowed to operate internationally. i shall therefore vote in favour of the proposal for a directive as it stands.
in writing. the proposed directive aims to improve the use of rental cars, as the current system is complex and bureaucratic. the most important change i see is the abandonment of the still existing and often used possibility of limiting the use of hired vehicles for transport on own account. this solution was criticized in the european union, including in poland. so it is only right that we step away from him. in addition, the use of a vehicle hired in another eu country is to be allowed for up to four months in order to allow companies to react quickly to temporary increases in demand for their transport services, which occurs, for example, seasonally in the transport of agricultural products. in addition, this solution will allow the efficient replacement of damaged vehicles with newer vehicles. the amendments proposed are therefore in line with the expectations of carriers, including polish carriers. they will improve the efficiency of road transport, which will also be beneficial for the environment.

in writing. – late payments remain one of the problems of the european single market. in europe, six out of ten businesses receive payments after the deadline set in a contract. while larger companies have the capabilities and financial means to cope with these difficulties, for smes and start—ups it might represent an existential constraint. delays in transaction have a negative influence on enterprises’ ability to invest, grow, plan production and pay their employees’ salaries, and it hinders their general financial health. in the worse cases, delays might lead to bankruptcy or debts. therefore, i am closely observing the implementation of the late payment directive, under which businesses must pay invoices within 60 calendar days and public authorities within 30 days. furthermore, the directive introduces automatic payment of interest for exceeding the relevant payment date. i believe that authorities and business organisations should promote a culture of prompt payments within their guidelines, sharing the best practices processes and, if necessary, legislate. settlement of missing payments cross-board should be simplified thanks to a european small claims procedure. a healthy business environment is a pre-condition for securing the competitiveness and solvency of the european economy.

in writing. while gender equality is one of the core values of the european union, women are still a significant minority on company boards and supervisory boards despite continuing efforts to increase gender diversity in key national bodies. today, women hold 15 percent of board seats globally. in poland, women hold just over 15% of the seats on supervisory boards and 6.3% of the boards of directors of over 480 companies listed on the main market. in the european union, the introduction of parity rules in some member states has proved successful. however, data collected by the european institute for gender equality show that in 2017, women accounted for only 25% of all board members of the largest listed companies in the eu, with large disparities between member states, ranging from 7,4% to 43%. this clearly shows the importance of the eu directive. that is why the council's position on this matter is so deeply disturbing. although the european parliament adopted its position as early as 2013, when it supported the commission's initiative to address inequalities by requiring at least 40% of women on company boards, the directive is still blocked in the council despite numerous calls from our side.

in writing. the union has been enacting legislation since the early 1990s to protect endangered animal species in the union and their natural ecosystems. this includes the birds and habitats directive. as a result, a number of animal species that were on the verge of extinction in europe have started to recover dynamically. this is especially true of large predators such as wolves, bears and lynx. initially, the mountain and peripheral regions were the main affected. however, the problem is now becoming more widespread: predators are attacking livestock and even humans, even in densely populated areas. wolves are particularly troublesome, causing increasing losses for farmers, forcing them to close their herds and investing in costly safeguards. but the biggest losses are caused by wild animals that destroy crops on a massive scale. cormorants and otters are also the main sources of damage in aquaculture. there is no doubt that the union's environmental policy is necessary and is producing tangible results. however, solutions need to be found to ensure a balance between the protection of endangered species and agricultural activities.

president-in-office of the council. – mr president, i am grateful for the opportunity to make a contribution to the discussion on the fair taxation for a just society, which is a very important topic for all of us. a year ago the european parliament had a topical debate on a similar question. this proves that we want, and we have to address tax issues on several occasions. while the eu needs to guarantee the prosperity and well-being of its citizens, collecting tax remains one of the key means through which governments are able to address poverty and inequality at national level. some may say that the eu could do more in the area of taxation, but i’d like to recall the progress that has been achieved so far over the last few years in this area, and we assure you that the romanian presidency will continue work in this direction. allow me to recall first of all the anti-tax avoidance directive, which is a major success in the eu, providing for a comprehensive framework of anti-abuse measures aimed at ensuring that taxation will occur where value is created. there were also four significant extensions of the scope of administrative cooperation in the area of direct and indirect taxation. tax rulings issued to companies will not be a secret anymore. tax authorities are now able to receive and exchange information on country-by-country reports. administrative cooperation in the area of vat was also reinforced. fair taxation also depends on international cooperation. as you are aware, global cooperation is key to combating base erosion and profit-shifting. for the eu, the list of non-cooperative jurisdictions and the work at the oecd level on digital economy taxation are two examples of successful international cooperation that has been established and that is contributing to the objective of fair taxation. firstly, on the eu list of non-cooperative jurisdictions. aggressive tax planning through the offshore system is detrimental to fair taxation and to a just society. however, all countries are free to adopt the tax policy that suits their specific needs. tax policy is one of the key elements of national economy policy and each country has the right to choose tax incentives to make its economy more attractive. but when tax incentives are harmful, others should be free to adopt appropriate counter-measures. the eu member states operating through the code of conduct group were able to have a contribution to changing the behaviour of most of the tax havens. the council has always stated that listing countries is not an objective in itself, and that most fundamental is that jurisdictions which are key partners of the eu share the same standards of tax transparency and good tax governance. most of the more than 90 jurisdictions which were invited for a dialogue, and which are important partners for the eu, are adhering to the standards common to eu member states. i think this is a major achievement, and this work will continue. more jurisdictions will be invited to engage in a similar dialogue in the near future. secondly, on the digital economy, eu member states are working closely with the oecd to find a global and comprehensive solution to the challenges brought about by the digitalisation of the economy. a broad approach is needed, examining the key aspects relevant to combating base erosion and profit-shifting, such as where tax should be paid and how much. the eu is working hard on an interim solution. the digital services tax directive would fill the gap while the long-term solution is being negotiated. we are likewise acting in the domain of vat, where major progress has been achieved. besides significant improvements to the current system of vat, the council has now started its work on the definition system and on the definitive system. i am fully confident that member states will agree on a compromise. everyone agrees that the eu needs a better system of vat but a lot of technical work is required. i could continue with many other examples of good and promising work that are ongoing in the area of taxation. to conclude, i will stress the need for an honest debate on tax issues, and i am glad that we have a contribution to that today.
member of the commission. mr president, mr minister, ladies and gentlemen, hello to all, i am very pleased to have this opportunity to debate together again on a subject which is very dear to me, and to us, that of tax justice. it is almost five years since we took office and we are approaching the end of our term of office, both for parliament and for the commission. the time for proposals is coming to an end and it is time to assess the progress we have made towards tax justice in the european union. i would like to begin by thanking the european parliament, by thanking all of you for your support throughout this mandate. our two institutions have become natural allies in the fight against fraud and tax optimisation. we have exchanged very regularly, here and in brussels, in the context of hearings and various special committees (tax and pana), and the reports you have published have fed our discussions and reflections on tax justice. it was absolutely imperative to act to strengthen tax justice in the european union. in recent years, repeated scandals have exposed the shortcomings of our tax rules, which are clearly incapable of combating fraud and tax optimisation. in addition to the shortfall in our public finances, which is estimated at between 50 and 70 billion a year in the european union for vat alone, these scandals have given rise to a legitimate feeling of injustice among european citizens, who have asked us to react. we have heard their call and put tax justice at the top of the european agenda; i am convinced that we have put the european union at the forefront of this fight. since 2014, we have succeeded in getting 14 proposals adopted, including eight on fraud and tax optimisation. despite the lack of unanimity, this is more than in the last 20 years. our action has been based on three priorities. the first pillar of tax justice has been transparency. the lack of information is always, as you will have noticed, at the heart of tax scandals. fraudsters play on the culture of secrecy, the grey area that surrounds tax practices, and so i have acted to put an end to tax opacity in europe. perhaps our most emblematic proposal is the obligation of transparency for tax intermediaries. we are talking here about banks, law firms or consultancies, which are often the main architects of tax optimisation and which sell their clients tax schemes that sometimes border on legality. the directive will oblige tax intermediaries, as of 2020, to submit their tax planning schemes to their national tax administrations. the aim is not to monitor for punishment, but to give tax administrations the means to identify and correct shortcomings in their legislation. then we abolished the banking secrecy of the european union. the various tax scandals - i am thinking in particular of the recent revelations known as 'cumex' - have shown that certain companies, or certain taxpayers, took advantage of the lack of coordination between tax administrations to avoid paying taxes, and this had to be remedied. as of 2014, we have therefore made the exchange of information between tax administrations in europe a general practice and it is now mandatory and automatic in the vast majority of cases: each member state must transmit to all the others the essential information on accounts, on tax agreements between states and companies, and on taxes paid by multinationals in each country. finally, transparency requires the exchange of information, but also a stronger dialogue between member states on their tax practices and, as you know, the use of taxation as a means of attracting the wealthiest businesses and taxpayers is not unique to a few islands here and there. some countries in the union, let us not be afraid to say, advocate a fiscal framework in which tax competition is a tool for competitiveness. and while tax competition is legal, unfair competition is not, or rather should not be. we have tackled this problem head-on. last march, the commission identified for the first time seven member states whose tax systems are being used in the context of, say, aggressive tax optimisation schemes. it was a difficult process, but it was necessary because as friends, we have to tell each other everything. the aim is not to punish, not to stigmatise, but to help create a fair and modern tax framework that ensures europe's global competitiveness, while protecting the interests of europe's 500 million citizens. the second pillar of my action for tax justice has been the strengthening of international cooperation. we have long known that tax havens around the world are the essential relays for tax fraud and tax optimisation. in response, the 28 finance ministers adopted, for the first time, a blacklist of tax havens around the world. many were sceptical, many doubted the effectiveness and sometimes even the sincerity of our approach. however, a few months later it is clear that the european voice has been heard. almost all of the identified jurisdictions have made, and this was the aim, specific and credible commitments to move off the blacklist. the quality of a blacklist is not judged by its length, but by the efforts made to avoid being included. and i am continuing the discussion with third countries. i meet very regularly with many prime ministers and ministers who have never stepped foot in the door of the commission simply because they are afraid of the blacklisting process. it is extremely effective and we will present the results in detail. the european union has also established itself as a world leader in tax good governance. it was the first to adopt the oecd measures known as beps. it has translated them into its legislation, in the atad 1 and also, most importantly, atad 2 anti-tax evasion directives. we participate in the work of the oecd and the g20. today i am particularly interested in the proposals of the oecd working group, published at the end of january, concerning the revision of the rules on income taxation and the introduction, which i believe, of an effective minimum rate. we must move forward on this subject, we must follow these reflections very closely. the third and final pillar of my action for tax justice has been the modernisation of european tax rules. i realised early on that the obsolescence of european tax rules was creating intolerable situations of tax injustice and inequality. i have therefore embarked on a major project to modernise the european tax framework. the main aspects of this modernisation were, firstly, the definitive vat system, which could make it possible, i repeat, to put an end to crossborder tax evasion amounting to 50 billion a year and which would considerably simplify the lives of our companies; and secondly, the common consolidated corporate tax base, which would allow companies to operate in the single market as simply as within a single country, is also a very big project. another important element of my proposal is the taxation of digital activities. today, the profits of digital businesses, although huge, are taxed little or not at all in the european union. this is clearly unacceptable, and i have therefore put forward two proposals to ensure fair taxation of the digital economy in the european union. the first is to modernise the rules on corporation tax by introducing the concept of digital presence. and it will become even more important now that the oecd is looking for global standards. the second is the introduction of a temporary tax on the turnover generated by certain digital activities in the union. the commission's proposal has been on the table for ten months now and although we have succeeded in convincing a large majority of member states, namely 25 out of 28, a handful of reluctant member states are still blocking the way, and i regret that. on the one hand, because our fellow citizens expect us to put an end to this blatant injustice, and on the other hand, because some member states, including france, spain and the united kingdom, which is still a member of the european union, are beginning to move forward on their own. and it is a risk to the integrity of our single market. i would like to conclude with a further consideration. the 'digitax' case illustrates the limits of unanimity. i hope we will have an agreement in march. the romanian presidency is working on this, i thank it, but i know it is complicated. if unanimity is overwhelming when it comes to reacting to tax scandals and when public pressure is strong, it can paralyse when it comes to structural reforms (energy tax, climate change, digitax, financial transaction tax, consolidated common base, vat). that is why i have proposed here in the european parliament in strasbourg that qualified majority voting should be introduced in tax matters, by means of the bridge clauses which make it possible to transfer to qualified majority voting those areas where decisions are taken by the member states unanimously. in concrete terms, this would allow the european union to react more quickly and more effectively and would, in future, strengthen the democratic legitimacy of tax decisions taken in the european union. tomorrow, ladies and gentlemen, you must be aware that if the decision to move to qualified majority voting is taken, the european parliament will be a co-legislator and the interests of all europeans will be better represented. this seems important to me at a time when the desire for representation and the thirst for democracy among europeans are so strong. that is why - i know there are elections coming - i would modestly suggest to the political parties to look at this question: if there were a very large majority here tomorrow, in all the seats, to demand this passage, it would change the game. and some of the ministers i saw yesterday or at ecofin, who were very reluctant, could not ignore it. finally, it would broaden the scope of tax policy in europe. we could pursue broader social objectives, such as environmental protection, by taxing polluting activities or regulating financial markets or taxing financial transactions. i call on the european parliament to take up this proposal frankly, to keep the debate going - it will not end now - because it is also a way for this institution to strengthen its authority. i would like to thank the rapporteur for his excellent report, which i think is a very useful one. i regret today that we did not make full use of it, even though the need for justice is growing stronger among many europeans, four months before elections, the importance of which we all know, i call on the member states to take up these issues to send a strong signal to our fellow citizens and convince them, if necessary, even more of the usefulness of europe. but here we have a good case of europe's usefulness: without europe we cannot fight against tax fraud and evasion, and on behalf of the ppe group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. the customs union is one of the foundations of the european union as such. its efficient operation has a fundamental impact on the european union's finances, on the activities of businesses, on consumer safety, which is very important, but also on the european union's external trade with third countries, and - as this report is about - on competition, which is internal. it is therefore clear that we as the european parliament must not only look at the perceived efficiency of the functioning of the customs union, but also encourage the commission to modernise it. there are certainly some important challenges in this area. the first one, which has been talked about a lot here, is modern information technology. we're running late here. they must be eliminated, but i agree with the commissioner that the safety of new systems is the absolute condition, not the timing of their introduction. another issue is the unification of interpretation in the member states. we must have the same approach to the customs union throughout the union. and the last point, mr. chairman, which is obvious, but worth mentioning, is that the biggest challenge today is brexit. this will be a test for the european union in terms of customs union.
in writing. the customs union is one of the eu's earliest achievements and is essential to guaranteeing the eu's credibility and negotiating position in the area of trade agreements. in practice, the customs union means that the customs authorities of all 28 eu member states work together as if they were one single authority. they shall apply the same customs tariffs to goods imported into their territory from abroad and shall not apply tariffs on the internal market. the eu's single market would be impossible to achieve without the abolition of customs duties and the role played by the customs union in the supervision of imports and exports. standardisation of customs information and processes plays a key role in the harmonisation of controls, in particular with regard to phenomena such as misclassification and undervaluation of imported goods and misdeclaration of their origin. such errors are harmful to all economic operators, and in particular to small and medium-sized enterprises. customs authorities must strike the right balance between facilitating legitimate trade, customs controls protecting citizens, animals and the environment in europe, building consumer confidence in goods entering the internal market and the union's commercial interests. eu imports and exports amounted to eur 3 700 billion in 2017, and duties collected accounted for 15% of the eu budget.

mr. chairman, please! the polish thinker, stefan kisielewski, once said that socialism is a system in which heroically you fight problems that are unknown in any other system. and this discussion is a perfect example of that. it's like this: first, it starts with the fact that greedy governments try to collect as much tax as possible and therefore charge commissions on all the economic activity on their territory, and therefore they charge everyone with the obligation to record all this activity because they want to know how much they can squeeze out of everyone. this creates additional costs, business difficulties. it centralizes the market, it eliminates the smaller sellers, it introduces additional regulations that centralize the market, because centralization is convenient for the government, because it's easier for it to control it. the effect of this is ultimately to prohibit retail sales to farmers, weakening their bargaining power, resulting in unfavourable contracts and low purchase prices. the effect of this is not, as in our case, the withdrawal of these stupid regulations, but more regulations, so next time we meet to ask why agricultural prices went up. i can't wait to see it.

the question asked by raising the blue card. resolutions have been voted on many occasions in this parliament stating that the maintenance of small family farms is our priority here. you said a moment ago that the fragmentation of farms is the cause of the weak position of farmers. that's right, you're right. so how do you vote when parliament is passing such nonsense that it wants to maintain this inefficient structure of small farming?

in writing. on 19 december 2018, the austrian presidency and the european parliament reached an agreement on a directive to combat unfair trading practices in business-to-business relationships in the agricultural and food supply chain. the fundamental objective of the directive is to protect farmers, who are considered to be the most vulnerable actors in the food supply chain, from buyers who are much larger than they are. the directive will create a common european framework ensuring a minimum level of protection for farmers and other suppliers of agri-food products whose turnover does not exceed eur 350 million. the agreement covers food, cut flowers, pet food and animal feed. eight commercial practices will be completely prohibited, including: delay for perishable products, last-minute cancellation of orders, unilateral or retroactive changes to supply contracts, misuse of confidential information and retaliation or threat of retaliation against a supplier. all this is aimed at strengthening the position of smaller players (farmers) in the food supply chain.

'golden visas' are investor residence facilitation schemes that allow a third-country national to stay in a member state but also to travel freely within the schengen area. it is currently issued by 20 eu countries: bulgaria, croatia, cyprus, the czech republic, estonia, france, greece, spain, the netherlands, ireland, lithuania, luxembourg, latvia, malta, poland, portugal, romania, slovakia, the united kingdom and italy. in contrast, 'golden passports' are programmes that grant citizenship to investors on less stringent terms than usual, e.g. no physical presence or other actual ties to the country. the 'golden passports' are issued by bulgaria, malta and cyprus and cost between one and two million euros. golden visas and passports pose a threat to the eu as they create conditions conducive to money laundering, corruption and tax evasion and can undermine the effectiveness of international sanctions.

eu strategic communication to counteract hostile propaganda against it by third parties. i served as the ep rapporteur for the other report as well. the first report, adopted in november 2016, was divided into two parts. it indicated major actors in this work against the eu in the presentation of hostile propaganda. it was a state actor, namely the russian federation, and non-state actors, predominantly radicalised islamic organisations like isis. this time we decided to structure the report’s recommendations differently, thanks to the contribution of representatives of major political groups in the parliament. we divided the recommendations into parts, indicating the state of play in 2018 and targeting the hybrid warfare methods of this. we stress there the necessity to avoid censorship while countering the hostile propaganda, disinformation and misinformation that is presented to the eu and its member states. we stress the importance of quality journalism sustaining freedom of speech and freedom of the media. we also indicate the notion of possible legislative regulatory activity, at both eu and international level. there parties indicated the necessity to even introduce humanitarian law to deal with cyber—warfare or information warfare. we stress the changing patterns of a variety of actors. in terms of radicalised organisation, we mentioned that, instead of very popular websites that increased the level of radicalisation of young people, there are methods of encrypted messaging services that are very popular. much has been done, both within the eu institutions, eu-based institutions and organisations, and by civil society during those two years. we mention all of these activities in citations. i would like to stress the importance of the code of practice on disinformation, the activity of the european endowment for democracy (edd), as well as the transatlantic cooperation, and cooperation with like-minded countries and institutions like the transatlantic commission on election integrity on this. in the second part of this report, we focus on indicating types of misinformation, disinformation and hostile propaganda. the third part is dedicated to methods for safeguarding our elections. the current year, 2019, is the year of over 29 elections in eu member states, including the european elections that are to take place at the same time. after the experience of interference by the russian federation in elections and referendums in the eu and elsewhere, we have to strengthen our resilience to this kind of activity. we indicate the role of east stratcom and complement its activity, also indicating two other task forces for the western balkans, the middle east and the north african gulf area.

rapporteur. – mr president, the cooperation agreement on partnership and development (capd) between the eu and afghanistan was signed in february 2017, partially and provisionally entering into force on 1 december 2017. it was upon a council decision that the agreement remains a mixed one, meaning that both the eu and member states are engaged in the process of ratification. the security situation in afghanistan remains difficult, yet over 56% of the territory is under the control of the afghan government. that means that more than 65% of the population is also under the control of the government. since 2002, when the eu engaged in financing, more than eur 3.66 billion of humanitarian aid has been delivered in afghanistan. for the decade of transformation starting in 2015 we intend to deliver a further eur 1.4 billion to stabilise this country. efforts by the nato international security assistance force (isaf) operation and current resolute support with the participation of many countries, including my own, has brought development to the security situation, although, after the emergence of islamic state khorasan (isk), the daesh cells and groups that emerged following operations in iraq make this situation still vulnerable and fragile. the capd focuses on areas of relevance to the rule of the law, good governance, human rights, economic stabilisation and social stabilisation. we have to acknowledge and compliment the good achievements reflected in the statistics. access to health care has increased, due to european assistance, from 9% to 57%, a huge development. life expectancy has increased from 45 to 60. the level of education – schooling, access to schools – is much higher. voting patterns, in terms of participation in elections and the empowerment of women, also represent achievements in this country. the agreement was signed by vice—president / high representative federica mogherini and by the minister of finance of afghanistan, in the presence of the country’s president. we parliamentarians consider it regrettable that information about proceedings in the negotiation of the agreement came to this chamber considerably late, after the signing of the agreement. while our role is substantial, we participate, in accordance with the treaties, in the consent procedure for this agreement. i welcome and support it. i hope that it will be voted on positively.

in writing. despite their small size, andorra, monaco and san marino have always been an integral part of the european union's history and today enjoy strong economic, political and cultural links with many eu countries. it is high time to formalise these links i therefore welcome the ongoing negotiations on the association agreements. once completed, all three microstates will enjoy full participation in the internal market and the few remaining trade barriers will be removed. we must bear in mind the very limited administrative resources of each of these countries, as well as the enormous work involved in introducing legislative changes and implementing new legislation. it is therefore important to ensure that the burden of this is minimised. i hope that the negotiations will be concluded in the next two years as planned, and that andorra, monaco and san marino will enjoy even closer relations with the european union.
in writing. andorra, monaco and san marino are three micro-states that have always been part of the history of europe, not only because of their geographical proximity to the countries of the union, but also because of their shared political and cultural values. as a consequence of these countries' efforts to integrate more closely with the eu, negotiations for an association agreement were launched in 2015 and are now in their final stages. andorra, monaco and san marino have carried out important reforms and brought their legislation into line with eu law. it is therefore important to create an effective framework to facilitate the implementation of the association agreements in these three countries and to ensure a consistent interpretation of the eu acquis, taking into account their territorial dimension and social, economic and administrative implications. i hope that the negotiations will be concluded in the near future, which will in turn open the way for the agreement to be ratified by all the parties concerned.

on behalf of the enf group. - madam president! - i have to go. we're talking about the market. the mechanism of the free market is that companies and businesses that do not generate income go down, while those that best meet the needs of consumers grow. and it's through this mechanism that we can enjoy the abundance of goods. in a free market, there are really only two factors that determine success: consumer demand and low production costs. all administrative interference with the free market on the one hand helps those who are inefficient and should have failed to survive, and on the other hand imposes costs on those who have found a way to succeed and could have developed. the creation of an institution like the imf is another mechanism of very strong intervention in the economy, and this intervention is exactly contrary to the judgments of the free market. the result can be - and will be - only one: the growth of efficient companies will be stunted, and consumers will be burdened with financing companies that, as inefficient, should have failed. the creation of such a fund and the allocation of large financial resources to it also implies oligarchic privileges for large corporations, and any privilege granted to anyone is in fact discrimination against all others. so the mechanism of increasingly punishing efficiency and rewarding inefficiency is becoming more common. in this way, the union will provide europe with growth, but unfortunately with a negative sign. that's too bad.

mr president, first of all i would like to congratulate the commission for preparing this report and i’m convinced that we are taking an important step forward when it comes to the strengthening the economic and monetary union in the eu. the european monetary fund (emf) aims to replace and absorb the european stability mechanism as an efficient and key anti-crisis mechanism. it fills a significant gap in the existing system of governance in the euro area, in the first place. what are the tasks? first of all the emf would provide support to member states in financial distress. one could say that is the esm’s role, but this, as i will explain, is something which will be provided in a more efficient and prompt way. the second task is that it will serve as a backstop for banks that fall into financial trouble. so there is a chance that, by providing financing both to states and to the banks, we are finally going to break the vicious nexus of sovereign-bank connection. the mechanism will be fiscally neutral so it does give us a guarantee that it is not going to transform itself into a permanent payment transfer mechanism. further advantages include the fact that, in terms of governance, it is going to be much more efficient because, as part of the legal framework of the european union, the decision-making mechanism will be faster and it will be more willing and able to face crisis situations in member states. lastly, just one reservation: we should not consider the emf as a competitor of the imf, and i would urge the commission to design the whole solution in such a way as to still have access to, and to benefit from, the imf as an international institution.

the deputy rapporteur. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. last year we debated the revision of the regulation on jurisdiction, recognition and enforcement of judgments in to be welcomed. the european parliament supported the previous report by ms zwiefka by a large majority, pointing out several areas that were particularly important to us: the hearing of the child, the use of mediation in family matters and the placement of the child outside the family. it is welcome that all these issues have been addressed in the final text. this is especially important in the often difficult situation of a court decision to place a child outside his or her biological family. i would like to point out that it is still up to the court to decide whether the child will be placed in a foster home, a foster care home or with relatives, taking into account the child's background and the cultural environment in which he or she has lived. the new rules on cooperation between relevant services will allow reliable information to be provided and the court to decide in the best interests of the child. however, one should beware of misinterpreting this provision as requiring the courts to hand over a child of a given nationality to a family from the same country. it's still up to the court to decide that. new, more detailed rules and jurisdictional rules on parental responsibility are also a good solution. the court of the country where the child is habitually resident is still the starting point, but there are detailed exceptions. now, too, the consent of both parents may determine a change of jurisdiction, or the court with jurisdiction may decide that another court for the sake of the child may be more appropriate to hear the case. a new article in the procedure for the return of a child after parental abduction also appears, which refers to a decision to refuse the return of a child under article 13 of the hague convention. it concerns a situation where the court or authority called upon to extradite a child proves that return is impossible in the best interests of the child. these are the dramatic situations in which a child is physically, mentally, or sexually abused. it's a good document that clearly states the procedure to be followed. in addition, as requested by the european parliament, the procedure for enforcement, that is, the certification of recognition of a judgment given in another member state, has been abolished. although it took the council more than two years to reach a common position, the member states have been able to do their job. the council's text takes into account a number of possible scenarios that occur in child custody cases and in parental abductions, where often nothing is black and white. the text presented has been adapted to the complex life situations of our citizens, and especially children. in many places it is emphasized that the court is to take the best interests of the child as the primary consideration in making decisions. we should therefore support the draft report which i am presenting today on behalf of mr tadeusz zwiefka and which approves the council's final text.

in writing. the regulation on jurisdiction and the recognition and enforcement of judgments in matrimonial matters and on the removal of a child abroad establishes uniform rules in matters relating to divorce, legal separation or marriage annulment, as well as in matters relating to parental responsibility in cross-border situations. it allows judgments, authentic instruments and agreements to circulate freely throughout the european union. it also clarifies matters relating to children and the procedure for reviewing judgments in this field in other member states. in addition, the regulation lays down the conditions for the return of children who have been illegally removed to another eu country. in this respect, the regulation strengthens the return mechanism provided for in the hague convention, which is the main legal instrument governing parental abduction. it should be noted that it applies only to international abductions and detentions. there is therefore a need to further improve judicial cooperation between eu member states to cope with the increasing number of cases involving citizens in cross-border relationships.
in writing. last year we debated the revision of the regulation on jurisdiction, recognition and enforcement of judgments in matrimonial matters, parental responsibility and child abduction abroad. the european parliament overwhelmingly supported my previous report, pointing out a number of areas which were particularly important to us: listening to the child, the use of mediation in family matters and the placement of the child outside the family. i am glad that all these issues are included in the council's final text. this is especially important when the court decides to place the child outside his or her biological family. new rules on cooperation between relevant services will allow reliable information to be provided and the court to decide in the best interests of the child. i would like to warn against a misinterpretation of this provision, which would seem to require the courts to hand over a child of a given nationality to a family of the same country. it's still up to the court to decide independently, taking into account the background, the cultural background, and most importantly the best interests of the child. the council's text takes into account many possible scenarios that occur in child custody cases and in parental abductions, where often nothing is black and white. the text presented has been adapted to the complex life situations of our citizens, and especially children.

the rapporteur. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, the commission has been working on a proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment. i would like to thank all the co-rapporteurs very warmly. the general compromise was reached despite the initial significant differences of opinion. there are a few things that will come up in the vote tomorrow. it is important to look for sensible solutions, realistic solutions to implement, and unfortunately not everything is possible today because there are no real technical tests. we therefore ask the commission to undertake some of these tasks before the next revision of the directive. but what's important today? the transport sector accounts for one third of the union's energy consumption and road transport for 22% of total greenhouse gas emissions. tyres, mainly due to rolling resistance, account for 5 to 10% of the fuel consumption of vehicles. the new tyre labelling model will provide consumers with greener, safer and quieter vehicles and will help reduce emissions in the transport sector. this is a significant step forward. it requires full information to be provided to users on fuel consumption, wet grip, external tyre rolling noise. the updated label will inform you of the grip on snow and ice, which has not been the case before. for the first time, labelling and requirements are being introduced for truck and bus tyres, c3 tyres, which will allow retreading tyres to be covered in future, with a new method of testing their performance being required. this will increase efficiency and bring tyres into the circular economy, and we have called for a review of the directive to speed up the work and to require tests to assess the impact of tyre friction and the release of microplastics. it's important not only for the environment, but for the health of each and every one of us. new requirements are in place for the display of the label, including for distance and internet sales. these new requirements will radically improve the visibility of all information for consumers. the regulation also improves transparency and enforcement by introducing the obligation to register tyres in the product database. the same information should also appear on or be attached to the sales invoice for tyres sent to the buyer. the user will thus be able to better understand the products and compare them against the relevant criteria. the result is a transparent solution for consumers, accelerating the environmental quality and performance of tyres, making them healthier and safer.

in writing. the european parliament voted in favour of the digital single market directive, which its opponents call acta2. for months, it divided the inhabitants of european cities: it was supported by artists and publishers, opposed by some internet users, who considered it an attempt to censor the internet. on the one hand, the directive is really about tackling piracy in a broader sense. for example, all websites that copy the text of individual newspapers or other media in its entirety. on the other hand, these regulations are a scandal. internet users have been deceived, as the directive can directly restrict freedom of speech online. it's an attempt to silence and censor. the most controversial articles on the so-called acta2 are articles 11 and 13. the first provides for the granting of related rights to publishers, while the second requires the filtering of content on the portal for copyright purposes. in the context of acta2, there is also discussion of article 3 of the directive, which provides that data from publicly available resources may only be used by research institutions for scientific purposes, which is a deadlock for private institutions.

on behalf of the ecr group. - madam president! - i have to go. water is a substance essential to life and to the maintenance of homeostasis in the body. water is our common heritage, which we should respect and safeguard for future generations. in view of its limited resources, we should manage it rationally and pay attention to the need to save water every day. each year, between 250 million and 500 million cubic meters of water are wasted in large cities. that's enough to feed 10 to 20 million people for a year. some environmental organizations estimate that turning the faucet on when brushing your teeth in a household of four saves up to three gallons [900 l] of water a month. if our tap leaks and the water drips at the rate of one drop per second, we lose nearly 12,000 liters of water a year. the provisions of this directive therefore aim to further improve the quality of tap water by tightening up the maximum limits for certain pollutants, such as lead, pathogens or substances having a negative effect on the endocrine system. they'll also be monitoring the levels of microplastics. the new rules also guarantee better access to information. if we reduced our consumption of bottled water, european households would save around €600 million a year and - just as importantly - reduce plastic waste and greenhouse gas emissions. tap water is cheap and environmentally friendly, but it has to be super-high quality and it has to be monitored constantly. it should be possible to install free water dispensers in public places, including restaurants. so, moving towards a circular economy, promoting sustainable and resource-efficient drinking water management, which will help reduce bottled water consumption, will in turn reduce greenhouse gas emissions and marine litter. remember, water is life! and finally, the search for life in space begins with the question of whether water is a necessary component of biological life. let's take this information as a civilized warning.

on behalf of the ecr group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. the commission's initiative to establish common principles for the assessment of sustainable investments is clearly needed. consumers are increasingly turning to eco-friendly products - food or energy. they're increasingly interested in the impact of the products they buy on the environment, the climate, or the welfare of animals. these important incentives are often exploited by unfair producers, and harmonised methods for determining which investments are sustainable can bring tangible benefits and curb unfair practices. however, i think that there is a need for some caution in order for this framework for defining sustainable investments to work in practice. first of all, it doesn't make sense to say which investments are bad for the environment. we have a lot of regulations in the european union to limit the environmental damage of business activities. if someone does not break these rules, there is no reason to punish him. let's reward good practice instead. besides, there's no point in adding social evaluation at this stage. i am all for social justice and protecting workers, but it is better to limit ourselves to the environmental assessment for now, and only after gaining experience to see if we can evaluate the impact on workers' rights later. the econ and envi votes are a viable and balanced solution, avoiding negative elements that would jeopardise the successful implementation of sustainable investments. i urge you to consider it.
mr. chairman, please! today we are discussing an important report on the establishment of a framework to facilitate the financing of sustainable economic investment in the european union. the european commission has developed criteria to determine whether an investment contributes to the transformation of the european economy towards environmental and climate objectives. we have an ambitious task to tackle climate change, which is why i support the european commission's proposal. at the same time, however, i believe that the approach to sustainable finance must be realistic and based on technology neutrality. reducing greenhouse gas emissions should go hand in hand with preserving the competitiveness of european industry. we should consider the broadest range of technologies that support the fight against global warming. unfortunately, the proposal put forward by the rapporteurs threatens to eliminate a whole range of investments aimed at reducing co2 emissions. arbitrary exclusion of certain technologies will lead to a situation where sustainable finance will be limited to a very narrow group of investments and will not produce a scale effect. we cannot support solutions that a priori and administratively exclude entire sectors of industry from access to sustainable finance. i think our job is to create incentives and mobilize the industry to do low-carbon activities, not punish them. there's no need to stigmatize and punish entire sectors. the criteria for selecting sustainable investments must be objective, proportionate and based on scientific research, including market research. i therefore call on all colleagues to accept the report as it was voted on at the econ-envi joint committee meeting.

the rapporteur. - mr president, i have to say that i am very pleased with the report. the gas supply is the most delicate and difficult issue for europe's energy security. firstly, we have less and less of our own european gas and we use more and more of it, and secondly, until recently it was difficult to imagine a transparent gas market in the european union with competitive prices. it is essential that the rules of the internal energy market of the union apply throughout the union, including the territorial waters of the member states, which are very important in this case. what do these rules say? ownership, third party access, any pipeline, and non-discriminatory and fair tariffs. the new directive guarantees all this, and it is the end of the era of the monopolists on the european gas market, who either threatened high prices or even the turning of the gas cap. we are, in fact, 10 years behind, because the directive, the third energy package, was introduced exactly 10 years ago during the czech presidency in 2009. i would like to pay particular tribute to commissioner miguel cañete for taking the initiative to introduce this solution, and to the romanian presidency for having been very courageous in entering into the negotiations. following these negotiations, the supplementary gas directive covers all infrastructure outside the european union, i.e. all pipelines supplying the european union from third countries, but in particular newly built pipelines which have not yet been put into service. this directive is therefore not directed against any country or against any supplier of gas to the european union. if a supplier has a problem with this directive, it is more a sign of his intentions than of what we are introducing, because we are only introducing european law throughout the union. and one more important thing. we're voting tomorrow, and that's the end of the first phase of our efforts to have legal solutions, but now there's the implementation problem. this will depend largely on the european commission and the court of justice of the european union. if the european commission's action proves to be inadequate, parliament will monitor and monitor the implementation of eu law. we cannot and will not allow any gas pipeline which is harmful to our energy security or which is incompatible with the objectives of the energy union, i.e. with the principles and values, such as the diversification of sources and routes of gas supply, to be granted any facilitation or derogation under eu law. i am convinced that this is a the next item is the report by mr gérard depreza, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on enhancing the security of identity documents of union citizens and of residence documents issued to union citizens and their family members exercising their right of free movement (com ((2018) 0212 - c8-0153/2018 - 2018/0104cod)) (a8-0436/2018).
member of the commission. – mr president, our right as european citizens to move freely within the union is one of the most important achievements of european integration. it requires that the documents we use when exercising this right are secure and reliable. a number of member states still issue id cards that do not meet international standards. some even issue paper id cards and many such id cards remain in circulation. weak id cards represent a serious security gap. they can easily be falsified and could be used by terrorists and other criminals to enter the eu. that is why the commission proposed a regulation to strengthen security features for id and residence documents in april 2018 as part of a wider package of security measures. i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr gérard deprez, for his excellent cooperation on this initiative. his efforts to find acceptable and workable solutions were tireless and, in the end, successful. let me also thank all the shadow rapporteurs for their hard work and commitment. last but not least, let me thank the romanian and austrian presidencies for their efforts. i would like to stress that the regulation does not oblige member states to introduce id cards if they do not already issue such cards, nor does it make id cards mandatory in those cases where they are optional. in these situations citizens will continue to use a passport instead. also, the new rules on id cards cannot serve as a legal basis to introduce national databases containing citizens’ biometric data. regarding biometrics, i know there have been intensive discussions on whether id cards should contain a chip with the fingerprints of the holder and whether this should be compulsory for all member states that issue id cards. we have consistently argued that fingerprints are a necessary security feature. the inclusion of biometric identifiers, and particularly the inclusion of fingerprints, renders documents more reliable and secure, and having secure and reliable id cards is in the interest of citizens. fingerprints on id cards is also consistent with the approach for passports. many member states already include fingerprints in their id cards or may be planning to do so, but only an obligation at eu level can make sure there is no weak link in our area of free movement without internal border controls. at the same time, we agree with parliament that robust data protection and fundamental rights safeguards are essential. thanks to parliament’s efforts, the text makes clear that member states are fully responsible for the safe handling of citizens’ data. changes introduced by parliament will also make sure that the keys necessary to verify biometric data stored on the chip are exchanged between the member states. to summarise, the new common minimum standards will make sure that eu citizens can rely on secure and reliable documents. we fully support the compromise found by parliament and the council and look forward to tomorrow’s vote.
member of the commission. – mr president, i would like to thank the honourable members for their interventions and again, many thanks to the rapporteur and shadow rapporteurs. i’d like to make a very short comment related to the mandatory fingerprints. they were included in the preferred option as it was decided to give more importance to the criterion aimed at improving security. at the same time, there are several very important safeguards introduced in the proposal. the safeguards in the text ensure the protection of citizens’ personal data. in response to the requests by parliament’s representatives, many recommendations by the fundamental rights agency have been included in the text. as suggested by the fundamental rights agency and the european data protection supervisor, the text makes it absolutely clear that it does not provide a legal basis for databases for the storage of biometric data. we fear that the opinion of the european data protection supervisor might have been based on some kind of misunderstanding of the encryption used for fingerprints on the chip of id cards. contrary to what is stated in the opinion, the fingerprints on the chip can only be accessed by authorities with the necessary certificates. we believe that the safeguards introduced in the text ensure the protection of citizens’ personal data, and we welcome parliament’s effort in this regard. i am convinced that this piece of legislation is a very important contribution to our overall efforts to strengthen the security of our citizens. therefore, i would like to encourage you to vote in favour of the compromise text. it will make the lives of the eu’s citizens easier when exercising their free movement rights and it will increase the level of security in our union.
i'm closing the debate. the vote will take place on thursday 4 april 2019. the competent authority shall inform the applicant of the reasons for the refusal of the application.

mr. chairman, please! just a few generations ago, all the richest and most powerful countries in the world were here in europe, because they were guided by a basic economic sense. they were eager to accept products from areas where production and raw materials were cheap. europe was powerful and rich. now europe seems to be protecting against the influx of cheap manufacturing and even encouraging the increase in the cost of production in our country. so the european union is the slowest growing part of the world, and china is one of the fastest growing parts of the world. and interestingly, the chinese don't need europe for anything. they'll be fine without us. our problem in our economic relations with china is not china's behaviour but the behaviour of the european union, which with its regulations paralyses the economy and increases the cost of production in europe. and that is the greatest misfortune.
vice-president of the commission. – mr president, thank you very much for the very good debate. even though there have been some differences in views, i would say that that we have a relatively unified position which is attitude-free. by saying this, i mean that it’s not wise to have any particular negative attitude in our relationship with china; what is needed is an honest assessment of the current state of play. that’s why our communication is based on the assumption that our future relationship with china must be based on fairness, multilateralism and reciprocity. it’s supposed to be very easy to defend by everyone. as i said before, and as everybody should know, china and the eu are strategic partners. we have cooperated, and will cooperate, and want to cooperate with china very closely on various foreign policy-related issues – and also in security-related issues – upholding and enhancing multilateralism on trade. it’s also worth acknowledging that chinese companies are sometimes better than our companies. they can compete with our companies even without state subsidies. but it’s equally important to acknowledge that this is not always the case. we have to make sure that europe can improve its competitiveness, as china will be a major player in the global economy in the coming years, and we have to make sure that our economies can develop so that we can compete on an equal footing when there is a level playing field. even without china, we have to improve our competitiveness when it comes to innovations and other dimensions of competitiveness. china wants to be seen as a developing country. to a certain extent, it is a developing country. when looking at the number of poor people or at democracy or other dimensions of the society, there are features which we can acknowledge as features of a developing country. but, at the same time, it’s fair to say – and honest to say – that china is a military superpower, it’s a political superpower, it’s a technology leader, and it’s a market leader in some areas. that’s why we have to treat china as a normal competitor and strategic partner and cooperating partner. there’s nothing bad and unfair about expecting reciprocity. strategic partners are supposed to provide and base their cooperation on a reciprocal way to cooperate. multilateralism and rules-based systems are very often mentioned by chinese leaders, and when i have had a chance to cooperate with many chinese authorities and leaders, i generally believe that they believe that multilateralism is a good basis for international cooperation. having said this, it’s also honest to acknowledge that sometimes china is using multilateralism and a rules-based world order rather selectively. again, we as strategic cooperating partners must agree that multilateralism means multilateralism, a rules-based system means a rules-based system, and we have to make sure that reciprocity is respected. our relationship with china is very active, and we are willing to deepen this relationship in various fields. but, at the same time, whilst technology, the market and china have developed positively, there are new challenges in our relationship and we want to solve those challenges. we have not chosen the same way as the united states to deal with china. we want to be constructive but fair, and expect reciprocity.

the next item is the joint debate on the report by maria grapini, on behalf of the committee on the internal market and consumer protection, on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council establishing a programme of 'customs' cooperation in the field of customs (com ((2018) 0442 - c8-0261/2018 - 2018/0232 ((cod)) (a8-0464/2018)) and the report by jiří pospíšil, on behalf of the committee on the internal market and consumer protection, on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council establishing, under the integrated border management fund, financial support instruments for control purposes (com ((2018) 0474 - c278/2018 - 2018/0253 - 2018/08d (cod)) (a8-0604/2018).
the rapporteur. - mr president, i will follow up what the honourable member, mrs grapini, has said. yes, indeed, we are discussing today a very important report on the creation of a new financial instrument to finance the equipment of individual customs offices and thus strengthen the real foundations of the customs union. in short, there are now over 2 000 customs offices at the eu's external borders, with very different equipment, which in turn determines the quality of the checks carried out by these offices. this financial instrument, which would apply, as stated, to the next financial period from 2021 to 2027, is therefore intended to contribute to the standardisation of customs equipment in the future and thus to ensure that the controls carried out at the various points of the external border are the same, are in some way equally detailed and also guarantee a rapid control which does not interfere with the passage of goods across the border. it will not therefore affect international trade at the external border. this instrument, which seems perfectly logical in the light of the customs union, which is a european issue and not just a national issue, has to be said to have been proposed directly by the member states, the member states which are in charge of the external border. however, it should be noted that the draft regulation itself envisages that the funds would be drawn not only from the states at the external border but also from all the states which simply carry out controls on goods entering the eu. i am therefore, as rapporteur, very pleased that this instrument has been adopted and is being implemented, and i am convinced that it will eliminate the imbalance that exists today between the various customs controls, and the only chance is to have the same equipment and the same methodology of controls as those carried out at customs offices. it should be said that the commission's proposal for customs equipment is for eur 1.3 billion, which is a large sum at first sight, but when we consider that a scanner like this costs around eur 4 million, one such device, and when we consider that this is a multiannual financial framework, the amount itself is not that large. we have had a detailed debate on this in the imco committee and our message is not to reduce this amount but to try to increase it in the future. as mrs grapini has already said, the first reading did not include the classic trilogue and there was no political agreement, mainly because the current presidency is not authorised to negotiate the specific form of the financial framework for the years 2021 to 2027. the basis of political agreement on this financial instrument is to know how much money will be redistributed. if we do not know this, we are not able to reach a political agreement at the first reading. this was the view of the majority of the representatives of the political groups in the imco committee, and i eventually came to agree with this view, and therefore there is no political agreement in the trilogue. once it is clear in the autumn what the amount is for this programme, it will be possible to complete the discussion of the whole regulation and move on to the final stage. the benefits are clear, but it's important to know what money will be allocated to this program.

in writing. to deliver effectively on the priorities of the european union, the multiannual financial framework (mff) must both create new instruments and modernise existing ones. with this in mind, the european commission has proposed the creation of new programmes based on previous proposals from member states based on their needs for better management of external and internal borders. in may 2018, the european commission adopted the 2021-2027 mff package, in which it proposed a new integrated border management fund (ibmf), consisting of a financial support instrument for border and visa management and a financial support instrument for customs control equipment. the customs control equipment support facility aims to strengthen controls on goods imported into and exported from the eu by providing financial resources for the purchase, maintenance and modernisation of customs control equipment (scanners, automatic identification systems for registration numbers, portable laboratories for the analysis of samples). i agree with the rapporteur that there is a need to clarify the issue of the use of customs control equipment by other entities for additional purposes, so that there is no abuse that hinders the achievement of the objectives of the instrument.

vice-president of the commission. – madam president, thank you for organizing the debate today to speak about digital taxation and in particular the fate of the digital services tax, where a council agreement has not been possible. on digital taxation, i know you have been vocally supporting our proposal and i would like to thank you for this. let me start my intervention by briefly recalling why the commission presented an initiative on this issue on 21 march 2018. we did it because the underlying reasons remain valid and the problems that we are trying to fix remain unsolved. this has to be kept in mind while working on this issue during the upcoming months. after all it’s simple, international corporate tax rules are no longer adapted to realities of the modern global economy. they do not capture the benefits derived from digital services when there is no physical presence in the country. the consequence of this inability to apply our current tax rules to these new realities is clear. today profits from certain digital activities are barely taxed in the eu and this is unacceptable. it threatens the long-term sustainability of our public finances. it disrupts the conditions of competition for businesses in our single market and it undermines the fundamental principles of tax fairness. this is why we have proposed two ways to ensure fair and equitable taxation of the digital economy. firstly, a structural proposal to reform the rules on corporate taxation so that profits are recorded and taxed where companies interact significantly with users via digital channels. this is a comprehensive solution. secondly, a more targeted proposal that responds to requests from several member states for a provisional tax on the main digital activities that currently escape any form of taxation in the eu – the digital services tax. this is an interim solution to apply until the comprehensive solution is agreed. as you know, council discussions have mainly focused on this interim solution and we are obviously disappointed that member states have not been able to reach a unanimous agreement on a proposal for the digital services tax, despite the fact that there was a large majority of member states in favour. the failure to reach unanimous agreement on this file is largely explained by unanimity rule, according to which council must decide unanimously on proposals in the area of taxation. as explained in this year’s communication on qualified majority voting, this is just another example of many tax initiatives where the unanimity requirement has hampered the progress needed to strengthen the single market and avoid its fragmentation. in today’s larger, modern and more integrated eu, a purely national approach to taxation no longer works and unanimity is not an effective way of decision-making. this is why we have launched the debate around this topic. in any event, i believe that the complex work that has led us to the near compromise on the digital services tax has not been in vain. firstly, it will provide a framework for our member states which decide to move forward by adopting an interim solution at national level. secondly, we will be able to examine the proposal on the table of the council if the g20 and the oecd on the reform on the corporate tax system have reached no international agreement in 2020. moreover, the proposed digital services tax has the merit of having accelerated international discussion within the oecd and the g20 on the comprehensive solution. as you know, in march 2018 the oecd delivered an interim report in which it committed to reach a long-term consensus—based solution on the tax challenges arising from that digitalisation of the economy and the remaining [inaudible passage]. we strongly believe that the solution to tax and the digital economy must ultimately be a global one. we have to keep up the momentum for the g20 finance ministers discussions last year. i will continue to work and engage with the international community and it will be important to coordinate the european efforts in the oecd. speaking with one voice will allow the eu to put more pressure on the discussions and better defend our interests. it will be important that in our efforts to modernise corporate tax rules, we avoid repeating mistakes from the past, creating new layers of complexity cannot be a way forward. we need to think of a system that is simple and future-proved. this should not patch the system but really reform it.

in writing. europe is and should remain at the forefront of pharmaceutical research and development, and the spc also supports europe's pioneering role in pharmaceutical research and development. these rules foster creativity and allow the pharmaceutical industry to maintain its world-class innovation potential. i therefore fully support the proposed exception for the protection of spcs as a way to remove the unintended legal obstacle that has prevented eu-based generic and biosimilar manufacturers from competing in export markets where competition is known to be fierce and to restore a level playing field for eu and non-eu manufacturing. supplementary protection certificates (spcs) extend the patent protection of medicinal products which must undergo long-term tests and clinical trials before they can be marketed. the exemption will allow eu-based companies to produce a generic or biosimilar version of a protected medicinal product in the future during the period of validity of the protection certificate, if this is done solely for export to a market outside the eu where protection has expired or never existed.
in writing. the aim of the new rules is to level the playing field on the world market for small and medium-sized eu pharmaceutical manufacturers, while maintaining the protection of manufacturers of generic medicines. these are very important changes for polish pharmaceutical manufacturers. until now, spc protection has covered both the sale and manufacture of a generic medicine throughout the eu. however, pharmaceutical companies located outside the eu can manufacture and sell a medicine worldwide outside the eu after 20 years of patent protection, and can also enter the eu market with a generic once the five-year protection period has expired. this puts smaller eu companies at a disadvantage. the leveling of opportunities in third markets will allow eu small and medium-sized pharmaceutical companies to raise capital to not only produce in the generics and biosimilars sector but also to build their own r&d facilities for the production of new medicines. in addition, they will not be forced to move production outside the eu, which will of course create new jobs for highly qualified staff. the changes are also intended to ensure that patients have faster and wider access to safe generic medicines produced in the eu once the spc protection has ended.
