in writing. the regulation on co2 emission standards for heavy-duty vehicles is part of the european union's integrated approach to decarbonising the transport sector. these regulations will undoubtedly pose a problem for both vehicle manufacturers and fuel dealers in the long run. the calculation methodology shall assign the co2 emission value of the vehicle to the vehicle based on the measured amount of co2 emitted from the vehicle's exhaust pipe. however, this does not include the total co2 emissions including those from the previous energy-intensive processing of crude oil as a primary energy source or from the production of renewable fuels, including biogas. the issue of reducing emissions from the use of biofuels and alternative fuels should also be addressed. the energy efficiency of the propulsion units is an important issue, as an increase of one percent reduces co2 emissions by up to several percent. however, the increased efficiency of diesel engines may result in an increase in nox emissions. in view of all this, the european commission should develop a better methodology for an objective and comprehensive way of calculating co2 emissions and avoiding nox emissions. the new methodology for advanced and renewable fuels should allow for further, substantial co2 emissions reductions. it will also allow companies specialising in the manufacture of heavy-duty vehicles to make bold use of new, lighter-weight materials and promising and competitive design solutions.
the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, i would like to thank you for your work. today we are summing up the extra-judicial work on the directive on the promotion of clean, low-emission vehicles. the question of why we need this directive is justified by the initiative of the european commission, because nearly 60% - some say as much as two thirds - of the emissions that cause smog come from road transport. and the public sector needs clean, energy-efficient buses, trucks, vans, but also specialized equipment that gives them a chance to deliver good public services. the european industry needs a long-term stimulus to introduce new public procurement regulations and respond to these challenges. we are adopting a set of ambitious targets today, and in the work we had to make sure that the height of these targets was achievable by future contractors, i.e. mainly local governments, and at the same time did not affect the limitation in terms of public communication. that is why it is so important that the directive be supported by the eu budget and the european financial institutions, especially for the purchase of this transport, which will meet the objectives of this directive. the targets in the directive are tailored to the economic capabilities of individual member states, although we hope that as clean technologies are introduced more widely, many member states will exceed these targets. however, they do not cover 100% of purchases, leaving room for other, more traditional technologies, e.g. hybrid vehicles, as only plug-in hybrids will meet the clean vehicle standard. local governments have told us that hybrid solutions are a good bridge from traditional to low and zero-emission solutions, which allows, among other things, to train staff, to acquire the necessary know-how for further changes, to build infrastructure. as part of these objectives, we have taken care to ensure as much flexibility as possible in the use of low-carbon technologies. linking the definition of 'clean vehicle' to the alternative fuels infrastructure directive, because that is the existing legislation. i thank the commissioner for her frankness in introducing this definition. the targets in the directive apply to both heavy and light vehicles. we are aware that the main effect of the directive will be on the bus market and its use in public transport. the vast majority of purchases are public tenders and will therefore be covered by the directive. and it is the buses that have the highest purchase targets imposed by the directive, but at the same time it is the bus manufacturers that have the most advanced low-emission technologies. and in the union too, we have champion manufacturers who have developed technologies and are successfully competing with their products on the european and world markets. for example, solaris, a company in the greater poland region where i come from, produces both zero-emission electric buses and hydrogen buses, which find buyers in europe and beyond. we hope that the use of low-emission technologies, including gas mobility, including natural gas, biomethane and liquefied gas, will allow for a rapid reduction in emissions from public transport through the emission of pollutants such as nitrogen oxides. it will also make better use of, for example, biogas, which we will be able to obtain in large quantities from organic waste in the future, as we have written among others after my proposal in the european circular economy. we know that the future of transportation is zero-emission, battery-powered, hydrogen-powered, we know that these technologies will be perfected. but new technologies also pose not only technical challenges, but also social and environmental ones. we must remember that battery production also has an environmental impact and leads to negative impacts also where we obtain minerals for their production. so we need to accelerate the development of sustainable battery production and batteries that can be used more widely, reused first by extending their life, and then recycled. batteries that use fewer critical raw materials, including rare earth elements the directive is intended to provide a long-term impetus for the development of the european industry, particularly in the field of battery technologies, including clean batteries. the union must develop technologies so that our industry can offer vehicles that are competitive in price and technology in the world, so that jobs, research and technology remain in europe, and so that public money is spent to support the development of european industry. i thank all my colleagues and counter-rapporteurs, with whom we have often had differences in the course of our work, but we seem to have managed to reach a good agreement. i would like to thank the european commission, which helped to reach a good compromise at crucial moments, and also the romanian presidency, whose decision has made it possible to bring in writing. transport today accounts for almost a quarter of the eu's greenhouse gas emissions and is the main cause of air pollution in cities. the aim of low-carbon mobility is therefore justified, as it is a prerequisite for the transition to a low-carbon economy that promotes environmental improvements. the transport system needs to be optimised and made more efficient, including through the promotion of multimodal transport and advanced biofuels. however, it is important to remember that the quality of infrastructure and the development of transport systems such as public transport, rail and inland transport are important. the commission is also proposing a new definition of clean vehicles and a transition period until 2025, after which much stricter requirements will be enforced on vehicles in the european union. the lack of financial support is a barrier to transport modernisation. it seems that the european commission should provide much more financial support for clean vehicles under the structural funds and the ce programme. it is the only way to improve the state of the environment in europe.
the rapporteur. - madam president, i would like to thank you. thank you so much for giving me a voice. i would like to thank you for your kind words. we are already feeling the end of the mandate and we are still to adopt extremely important documents, documents that the european market and european businesses are really looking forward to. i would like to begin by thanking commissioner jourová very warmly and, on her behalf, thanking the whole team who have drawn up an excellent draft directive, which has considerably reduced working time in both parliament and the council and has enabled the negotiations to proceed in a truly calm manner during the trialogue. i also wish to thank all my shadow rapporteurs and colleagues who have been actively involved in the project. what's it about? we're talking about company law, which is almost insanely important if we're talking about the functioning of the european single market and something that is the essence of modernity, which is digitization. in fact, this directive opens up new possibilities for the registration of companies by using digital technology and the internet. it is astonishing that it is only at the end of this term, a term that is really marked by digitalisation, its various aspects and the information society, that we arrive at the regulation that entrepreneurs and european companies are waiting for. ladies and gentlemen! i want to make it very clear that the aim we set ourselves was to improve and facilitate the functioning of entrepreneurs and companies in the modest context of company registration. the lack of such rules on registration, publication of documents or the lack of coordination between the different systems in some member states where this possibility already existed has led to increased costs, increased time for these procedures, and also a certain legal uncertainty when it comes to registration in another member state, which has sometimes led to a loss of market opportunities. at that time, such a company may not have been established or may have had to abandon various types of contracts because of the length of time required to register. the document before us will shorten that time considerably. this means that it will be possible to make such a digital registration within five to a maximum of ten working days. of course, this is subject to the requirements of the country of registration: all the required documents must be submitted and the conditions laid down in the directive must be met, which are intended to combat or even prevent possible fraud. this is a very important issue. ladies and gentlemen! how many companies could this be? well, according to the data i have, there are about 24 million companies in the european union, of which about 80% are limited companies, and almost all of them are small and medium-sized enterprises, which are the companies that generate the most jobs. so it's our job to make it easier for these companies to operate by saving time, money, and personnel costs. we are doing that by submitting this report. as i said, for the time being the rules will apply to companies with share capital, but i hope - and here i am addressing commissioner jourová - that when the review which we have started in about six years is completed, once it has been completed, the rules will be extended to all types of companies. ladies and gentlemen! i would also like to emphasise one more element, namely the need for cooperation between member states in implementing certain aspects of the directive, for example, concerning the holding of management positions or the determination that a person can hold a management position in a company. because it's a very complicated issue, we've even extended the implementation time of this directive a little bit. it is true that it brings some complications, but in the end it can only bring benefits, and any member state that implements the rules in the way we expect will soon be able to see this, and our european businessmen will certainly see it. i therefore urge that we vote to close the first reading tomorrow.

in writing. as a member of the european parliament for 15 years, i have had the satisfaction of seeing our work on harmonising the different national laws translate into tangible economic effects and the integration of the eu market, and more recently the digital market. the rules adopted today will simplify procedures for setting up companies abroad, i.e. in other eu countries, and will significantly reduce the time it takes to register them, without requiring a personal visit to the offices. the internet registration and the possibility to submit the necessary documents electronically is now a necessity and guarantees a modern and transparent space for the development of eu companies. the proposed rules do not alter the conditions for registration in the member states, i.e. they will not have a negative impact on the prevention of financial fraud or the participation of notaries in the registration process. once all the necessary documents have been submitted, the whole procedure should take no more than 510 days, depending on the type of company and whether the applicant is a natural or legal person. the draft directive also provides for the application of the 'once-only' principle, which means that documents and information will be submitted by the trader only once. this is the last plenary session of the eighth term of the european parliament. i have attended all the plenary sessions over the past three terms and now, as i leave the european parliament, i am pleased to have been involved in many innovative solutions to make life easier for citizens and businesses in our community. thank you for working with me.

member of the commission. – madam president, (inaudible) covered bonds are a stable and cost effective source of financing. they fared well during the crisis, while other sources of funding dried up. they are very popular in some member states and in others they are barely news. so the commission proposal seeks to develop this market further by drawing on the high standards and good practices of national systems. it is a key building block of the capital markets union to encourage investment and lending in the eu. the new rules will establish a pan-european covered bond market that supports lending to the real economy without disturbing already established and well-functioning national markets. they will boost the issuance of covered bonds also in member states where markets are less developed. these rules will help banks access a broad range of safe and efficient funding tools which in turn will allow them to finance companies and households. we estimate that the potential saving for borrowers will be around eur 1.5 billion a year. the new rules also set out to harmonise prudential rules for these instruments in order to contribute to financial stability. the new framework is based on two pillars. so, first the directive provides a common definition of covered bonds. it outlines the features of the instruments and it identifies the high-quality assets that can be eligible to back a covered bond. the directive establishes sound supervision for covered bonds as well, and sets out the rules allowing the use of the ‘european covered bonds’ labels. and the second, a regulation, strengthens the conditions for granting preferential capital treatment to covered bonds purchased by banks. as promised during the trilogues and set out in the commission’s statement accompanying today’s acts, the commission is willing to amend the liquidity coverage ratio, delegated act, in order to cater for the specific situation of covered bonds. this amendment will address the overlap between the cover pool liquidity buffer set out in the directive and the liquidity buffer foreseen in a liquidity coverage ratio. for this purpose, a declaration from the commission will be transmitted to the parliament before voting tomorrow. i wish here to thank the parliament for this successful outcome, in particular the rapporteur, mr lucke, and all shadow rapporteurs. the objectives of the commission proposals are largely maintained thanks to the effective approach of the parliament negotiating team and the good cooperation with the council. the transposition and implementation of the new rules on covered bonds should now proceed rapidly. this will ensure that this important source of funding can be used in all member states, thereby promoting jobs and growth throughout the eu.
on behalf of the ppe group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. i'm not going to let you down. we are debating two pieces of legislation today that establish the legal framework for the asset-backed securities market. for the sake of translation, i want to say that in polish terminology, these securities are called bank pledge notes. the market for bank-backed securities is an important element of the capital union we are building. i am glad that the negotiations between parliament and the council have resulted in a good compromise. the directive introduces a uniform definition of european asset-backed bonds, specifies the types of assets that can be used as collateral, lays down banking supervision obligations and the method for calculating the current value of assets. the directive also introduces two categories of bonds: european bonds, which meet the requirements of the directive, and european premium bonds, which additionally meet the requirements of the crr. the directive allows member states to determine the structure of the asset pool, including the size of the liquid assets holdings. in addition, in the regulation this was a very contentious point we reached a compromise of eight percent of the limit for collaterals in the form of third-tier credit quality assets. this framework harmonisation makes bank bonds a very safe, very high quality security, very attractive to potential investors. they are also a very convenient source of funding for banks. i congratulate mr bernd lucken on his excellent report and thank him for the cooperation we have had with him on this report. i thank the european commission and i thank the commissioner for her constructive contribution to the report and i appeal to all my colleagues to accept the report without amendments.

the next item is the debate on: question for oral answer to the council by danuta maria hübner, on behalf of the committee on constitutional affairs, on the negotiations with the council and the commission on a legislative proposal concerning the european parliament's investigatory powers (o-000003/2019 - b8-0019/2019) (2019/2536(rsp)) and question for oral answer to the commission by danuta maria hübner, on behalf of the committee on constitutional affairs, on the negotiations with the council and the commission on a legislative proposal concerning the european parliament's investigatory powers (o-000004/2019 - b8-0020/2019) (2019/2536(rsp)).
author. – mr president, the right of inquiry is a fundamental weapon for any modern parliament to make the executive accountable for their actions. if we think about mad cow disease, tax fraud on cigarettes, dieselgate or the panama papers, we understand that it is fundamental that parliament has a solid and sharp power of inquiry. ramón jáuregui said that the council and the member states systematically refused to sit at the table and have a real discussion on the content of the european parliament’s proposal. their argument was that the proposal of the parliament did not take into consideration their fundamental concerns. but this actually means ignoring the nature of the special legislative procedure established by article 226 tfeu. this procedure implies that the institutions exchange views and search for a compromise acceptable for all of them. the council demanded that the initial proposal of the european parliament should already contain the text acceptable for the council. this is not the way the consent procedure functions. how would the council or the commission react if the european parliament refused even to discuss possible ways to reach an agreement on, let’s say, the mff, using the pretext that it does not like the proposal of the commission? moreover, this attitude is not compatible with the principle of sincere cooperation between the institutions that we all should respect and cherish. at stake here is a fundamental question of respect for the prerogatives of the parliament and for the institutional balance. it is fundamental that the council and the commission understand it. at the end of the day, we do not have an obligation to agree with each other, but we have the duty to try. sadly, member states have not lived up to their duty.
member of the commission. – mr president, i would like to thank honourable members for all their comments and remarks. let me reiterate again that the commission attaches great importance to parliament’s role of scrutiny and political control, of which the ultimate aim is to guarantee that citizens’ concerns regarding the implementation of union law are properly addressed. the commission again recognises the work done by the institutions so far and acknowledges that the non-paper represents certain progress compared to the earlier proposals. at the same time, as i mentioned earlier, the commission still finds that the latest informal proposal contains a number of legal and institutional concerns, such as sanctions, investigative means and legal remedies. the commission acknowledges the need to have an adequate instrument which fully respects institutional prerogatives and the relevant legal frameworks of the member states. the commission is willing to engage in a constructive trilateral discussion with a view to finding appropriate solutions to the concerns that still exist. we hope that progress can be made on this politically sensitive, but very important, file.

vice-president of the commission / high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. – mr president, on 3 april brunei darussalam went on with the implementation of the 2013 penal code order. the court foresees, as you mentioned, punishments such as amputation, public flogging and death by stoning, which simply have no place in the world. also, there is a clear expansion in scope for the potential application of the death penalty, and you know our principled, clear, strong position against that penalty everywhere in the world. we believe there is no justification for these kinds of punishments – no crime justifies an amputation or torture, let alone the death penalty and, for sure, no person should be punished for loving someone. that can never be interpreted as a crime. these punishments – if applied – would constitute a violation of many of the international commitments undertaken by brunei darussalam. these acts are prohibited by the convention against torture and other cruel, inhumane and degrading treatment or punishment, which was signed by the country in 2015. they also go against the 2012 asean human rights declaration and they may also breach the country’s obligations as a party to the convention on the rights of the child and the convention on the elimination of all forms of discrimination against women. on the very day of the announcement, we reacted together with many of our international partners, starting with the un high commissioner for human rights, michelle bachelet. we expect now the government of brunei darussalam to make sure that the implementation of the penal court order will not infringe human rights and will be fully consistent with all international human rights obligations undertaken by the country. i think this debate is a very important opportunity to stress the expectations we have. we also expect the country to maintain its de facto moratorium on the use of the death penalty. let me add that we have been following this issue for years. it is not just a few weeks ago that we started to react. when the 2013 penal code was adopted, we suspended negotiations on a partnership and cooperation agreement with brunei, and since then we have raised the issue in all our meetings with the country’s authorities and in our annual reports on human rights and democracy in the country. it is now essential to prevent the application of such punishments. to this goal, we will first and foremost continue to put pressure bilaterally on the authorities of brunei, both directly and through the member states that are present in the country, and obviously the new eu special representative for human rights, eamon gilmore, will work on this. we will also continue to engage at the un human rights council, in particular within the ongoing universal periodic review, where brunei will be reviewed, and we will raise the issue with our asean partners, since this also represents a violation of a commitment taken by brunei in the asean framework. i will also have the possibility to raise this matter personally at our next annual european union-asean meeting next august. the ban on degrading punishments is not simply about european values. i want to underline this point that many of you have raised: these are universal values cherished by people of all backgrounds and of all faiths all around the world. these are rights that are not at the disposal of any authority or any country. they belong to all people and no state can take them away. this is about the dignity of each member of the commission. – mr president, i think we all agree that rain forests are a vital resource for the planet. this debate has reiterated that the ongoing fires in the amazon basin are deeply worrying to all of us, all the more so against the backdrop of devastating fires raging in other parts of the world. many have said – and i totally agree – that we have to tackle and we have to be concerned about all forest fires everywhere, whether it’s in angola, siberia, the arctic, the subarctic region, central africa, europe, southeast asia or south america. all these fires once more underline the sense of urgency required in joining our forces to fight climate change. forests are indispensable and are vital to our efforts to fight climate change. protecting forests is a significant part of our and everybody’s responsibility to meet the commitments under the paris agreement. most of the speakers spoke about the eu—mercosur trade agreement. in the trade and sustainable development chapter of the eu—mercosur trade agreement, both the eu and the mercosur countries, including brazil, accepted an explicit commitment to effectively implement the paris agreement. brazil’s nationally determined contribution under the paris agreement includes commitments on deforestation and reforestation. these are reinforced by private—sector initiatives, such as the soy moratorium or commitments by brazilian meatpackers not to source meat from farms in recently deforested areas. in addition to provisions to promote sustainable trade and the trade agreement itself, let me note that the trade deal is part of an overall association agreement covering dialogue on human rights and cooperation in many fields, including the environment and climate change. it will provide the eu and, indeed, the european parliament with additional instruments for dialogue and cooperation and help bring our markets and citizens closer together. many are concerned that we have to make certain that the commitments are there and that the commitments are honoured. the eu—mercosur agreement includes a comprehensive trade and sustainable development chapter containing legally binding commitments on environmental protection, as well as climate change, including a commitment to the implementation of the paris agreement. the commission has a range of tools and mechanisms available to ensure that these commitments are respected. where a party fails to comply with a commitment, we can resort to the dispute settlement mechanism, tailored to the specifics of labour and environment. we trust and expect, but above all, we will ensure that brazil will live up to its own commitments in the framework of the paris agreement, which includes a pledge by brazil to reduce by 2025 its net greenhouse gas emissions by 37% compared to 2005 levels, and an action plan to stop illegal deforestation, including in the brazilian amazon. on our part, we also committed a pledge by the eu to reduce our domestic emissions by at least 40% by 2030. some meps commented that we should also tackle the demand side regarding the marketing of products associated with deforestation. a legislative framework preventing products associated with deforestation to reach the eu market is key. it is essential. the eu already has domestic regulations banning, for example, the sale of illegally harvested timber. the main objective of the regulation is to reduce illegal deforestation and give consumers better assurances about the products that they buy. when it comes to any future eu domestic measures relating to products associated with deforestation, let me refer to our recent communication on deforestation where we have announced a number of other measures in this regard. those measures include reinforcing standards and certification schemes to identify and to promote deforestation-free commodities, exploring possible additional demand—side regulatory and non-regulatory measures to increase supply—chain transparency and to minimise the risk of importing products associated with deforestation and forest degradation, also, promoting forest-relevant considerations and activities to foster corporate social responsibility and responsible business conduct and, finally, establishing a stakeholder platform on deforestation allowing for discussions between government officials, ngo businesses, retailers, and so on. to conclude, let me remind everyone that the final legal texts of the association agreement and its trade aspect will be submitted to the eu member states and to the european parliament for approval.
president-in-office of the council. – mr president, to conclude i wish to thank you for this very useful debate on a pressing issue that concerns us all. we all share the view that we need to do our utmost to protect our forests. we need to improve the eu’s action on this matter and continue working towards honouring our international commitments. many of you referred to the mercosur trade agreement. the trade agreement with mercosur contains a robust trade and sustainable development chapter which lives up to the highest standards comparable to those in other modern agreements. the basic premise is that increased trade should not come at the expense of the environment or labour conditions; on the contrary, it should promote sustainable development. the mercosur agreement contains a specific article on climate change committing the parties to effectively implement the paris agreement. there are also commitments on fighting deforestation. however, just like here in parliament, discussions in the council on the eu-mercosur agreement are still in an early phase. it is clear that sufficient time will be needed for a comprehensive examination of the negotiated agreement. it will be important for both of our institutions to have an honest debate on the agreement, based on facts. i would also like to note that open, ambitious and rules-based trade policy which is value-based, sustainable and inclusive is a priority for the finnish presidency. many of you also referred to the urgency of climate action. the time to act on climate change is now, not later. we believe that the eu can have an effect on others by setting an example. this is why it is crucial to agree on an ambitious target of climate neutrality in the european union by 2050 as soon as possible. we must preserve the amazon rainforest for the generations to come. huge damage has been done so far, which i deplore, but we need to focus on preventing further deterioration. we need to protect our forests in the amazon and elsewhere because we need to protect our lives. deforestation is a global challenge with many complicated aspects. for that reason cooperation within the council configuration is an elementary part of successful work. the cooperation between the eu institutions is even more important and for that reason, we are all here today. thank you very much once again for your active participation and for your attention.
the debate is closed. written declarations (article 171 of the ccc)
in writing. governments that encourage the massive clearing and burning of rain forests must also consider the consequences. public opinion in favour of free trade with these countries may change. the fate of the amazon rain forest affects not only brazil but the entire world. that is why i support drawing attention to the problem and putting pressure on the brazilian authorities.
in writing. we express our full solidarity with the people of brazil and with the peoples of the other countries affected by the great fires in the amazon, in particular with the populations inhabiting the amazon forest. these fires are a dramatic example of what can happen when, as in capitalist society, the profit motive overrides basic environmental and social concerns. the destruction of the amazon did not begin just now. multinational corporations and other economic groups have long been vying for the resources of the amazon. this dispute finds expression in the economic, political and geostrategic spheres, and involves the appropriation of land, raw materials and resources extracted from nature. these objectives of appropriation and plunder of resources are found in the brazilian government, led by bolsonaro, ultra-liberal programs that give free rein and enhance the wealth of big capital and agribusiness economic groups, which aim to exploit the great natural riches of the amazon. the situation in the amazon region warrants international cooperation and aid to deal more effectively and more quickly with the disaster. but this does not legitimise those who have pretensions to favour plans and processes of economic domination and thus ways of transferring costs to the peoples of the world of environmental degradation, erasing the responsibilities of the capitalist mode of production.
in writing. the amazon rainforest is being destroyed on an unprecedented scale, with fires up 76% from last year. record-breaking fires, increasingly set by arsonists, the pollution of rivers by toxic waste from illegal mining, and the encroachment of indigenous peoples on their lands for mineral resources are destroying one of the world's largest tropical forests. it is important to continue and increase work to conserve rainforests, to ensure that their inhabitants and animals are protected and that natural resources are used wisely and not predatory. serious steps must be taken to preserve the amazon and to put out the fires that are currently burning there. the eu must also play its part.
in writing. we are alarmed by the state and recent spread of fires in the two main lungs of the earth. on the one hand, the amazon - the earth's first lung - has suffered a devastating wave of fires never seen before. these outbreaks have increased by 83% compared to the same period in 2018. the main cause? deforestation, which has also gained a strong impetus under the current government. on the other hand, the second lung of the earth, the forests of the congo basin, which recorded a total of 10 000 fires on the same dates. these two burning continents are a sanctuary for biodiversity and an essential tool in the fight against climate change. if the loss of tropical tree cover continues, it will be impossible to keep warming below 2 degrees celsius. we are concerned that governments such as brazil's have turned forest management policy on its head and undo all the progress the country had seen in recent years. political irresponsibility and poor forest management pose a great threat to our ecosystems and to our very survival.
we're having a debate after the meeting about the situation in the amazon. this is the area known as the lungs of the world (it produces 20% of the world's oxygen) and is crucial for tackling climate change. in contrast, large-scale fires that occur there have the potential to release large amounts of greenhouse gases into the atmosphere. i would like to address this question from the point of view of trade relations between the european union and the mercosur countries, namely brazil. it is certainly good that the proposed eu-mercosur agreement includes measures to combat climate change. on the other hand, we have seen the brazilian government and the president take a relatively lax approach to a disaster of this magnitude. it is also worrying that under the current president of brazil, deforestation in the amazon has increased by 88%, despite the fires. the draft agreement with mercosur aims to develop common trade relations. clearly, brazilian producers need a marketplace. on the other hand, our farmers are rightly concerned about brazilian production, which is massive and uses unacceptable methods. if this production is to be encouraged at the cost of the destruction of the amazon rainforest, that would be absolutely unacceptable. we must look at the agreement with mercosur through this lens and demand clear guarantees that its implementation will not mean the destruction of the lungs of the world and the reduction of the competitiveness of our farmers.
in writing. debates must finally be followed by action! we in the green group very much regret that the european parliament has not adopted a resolution on the forest fires in the amazon. the scale of the environmental disaster is clear: two weeks ago, mapu huni kuin from the brazilian state of acre warned us in the european parliament: 'the fires are destroying our livelihoods and our homes. we need the forest, it gives us freedom and our identity. at the political level, we need clear messages to bolsonaro and a multilateral solution in south america to stop the forest fires permanently!
in writing. the massive fires in the amazon region that have been raging for weeks have rightly raised great international concern. the fires do not appear to have been started accidentally, but are partly set on purpose to clear the land. forests are vital to us for many reasons. they are vital for biodiversity, climate protection and economic and social well-being. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment and the protection of the environment. we may have better tools for this in the future if the trade agreement between the european union and the mercosur region, which was reached in the summer in the form of a preliminary political agreement, can be successfully implemented. i therefore believe that the agreement should not be rejected, even though the brazilian authorities' actions have been, in the face of amazon's return, downright appallingly reckless. it is important to note that all new eu trade agreements, including mercosur, now include figures on sustainable development. it gives us the backbone to demand from our trading partners the maintenance of international agreements, cooperation and dialogue, including on environmental protection. it is very important, when the mercosur agreement is being discussed and worked on in the coming winter, to ensure that these objectives, which are enshrined in the agreement, are properly monitored and that they are also implemented in practice.

in writing. firefighters are a professional group that has consistently enjoyed the greatest, if not the greatest, public trust over the years. this is because, among other things, we can rely on firefighters not only for fires, natural disasters, and catastrophes, but also for many other hazards. a few months ago, right here in strasbourg, the law and justice delegation organized an exhibition that was an illustration of the true european solidarity of the heroic polish firefighters who last year helped to put out the fires in sweden. in my homeland, poland, volunteer firefighters play a huge role, especially in the daily lives of small, local communities. they are often the focus of not only rescue operations but also educational, cultural, and sporting events. this role has been recognised by the government of the republic of poland, which has provided statutory support to volunteer firefighters, which will allow not only the promotion of the principles of first aid but also fire protection and prevention. significant funding is also provided on a regular basis for equipment and training for volunteer firefighters. we know that they have saved lives and health on many occasions, and these values are priceless. their stand therefore deserves the utmost respect and support.
in writing. volunteer firefighters, volunteer rescue services and members of civil protection organisations play a very important role throughout europe and in hungary as well. they volunteer, in addition to their own work, in their free time to protect people's lives, health, material values, basic services for the population, the natural environment, natural values. their work, which requires serious expertise and is often dangerous, requires great determination, and their performance is admirable. the rules governing them, including their working hours, vary across the eu, along with national peculiarities and customs. however, it is important that this should remain the case, respecting the principle of subsidiarity, and that member states should be able to decide for themselves the conditions and hours of voluntary work and the length of the rest periods to which they are entitled. i would also like to take this opportunity to highlight that users of the emergency information system (eis), developed in hungary for smartphones and tablets, which is available nationally and free of charge, can obtain up-to-date information about the current situation in their place of residence, the areas affected by their destination, the routes monitored, the counties or even the entire country, about fires, accidents, power outages or warnings and alarms issued by meteorology. using the application, accidents can be prevented and user safety can be increased.
in writing. volunteer firefighters are undoubtedly a very important element in the rescue system of most eu member states. they are composed of trained men and women who, in the course of their duties, are often the first to offer victim assistance to the victims on the spot. they also work closely with other services to ensure the safety of citizens in their area of operation (city, municipality) or neighbouring areas. in the greater poland region, whose citizens have entrusted me with the mandate of mep, there are over 1 800 csr units with nearly 96 000 volunteers. although the majority of the teams are male, the women's teams are also very numerous, with over 2,500 members. it is worth noting that there are also more than 1,000 youth fire brigades in greater poland with 13,400 members, including nearly 5,000 girls. i believe the hard work of volunteer firefighters deserves the highest recognition. i am all the more concerned about the information on the risks that could result from the status of volunteer fire services in the european union. i am firmly convinced that we should do everything we can to ensure that the status of volunteer firefighters in the eu remains intact. moreover, the european commission and the parliament should bear in mind that the effectiveness of volunteer firefighters depends to a large extent on their having specialised firefighting equipment and being adequately funded.

in writing. legislative resolution on the council directive on the application of the principle of equal treatment between men and women irrespective of religion or belief, disability, age or sexual orientation adopted by the european parliament on 2 april 2009. it's been over 10 years. the lisbon treaty requires unanimity in the european council, but for a number of reasons member states cannot reach an agreement. for persons with disabilities, the eu ratified the un convention on the rights of persons with disabilities in 2010, marking a new beginning: the eu must fulfil its obligation under article 5 of the convention as soon as possible. it is therefore time to recognise that new approaches are needed to the horizontal directive. it is imperative that a prohibition of discrimination against certain groups, which is agreed between member states and, moreover, which is binding on the eu, cannot be legislated because of dilemmas faced by other groups. we will only make progress if we learn from our mistakes and do not try to force everything into a policy. i therefore call on the european commission to treat the disabled as a special group so that they do not suffer further disadvantages.
in writing. i consider the completion of the legislative work on the anti-discrimination directive to be a priority. especially since the council has been discussing it for a decade. in the union, we continue to see many cases of discrimination against individuals and certain social groups on the grounds of age and other grounds of unacceptable exclusion. unfortunately, national law addresses this problem in different ways. the directive would therefore harmonise anti-discrimination legislation at an appropriate level of protection. the lack of unanimity among member states is compensated for by the court of justice, which has made the principle of non-discrimination on grounds of age a general eu law (mangold) and confirmed its direct effect (kücükdeveci). the entry into force of the anti-discrimination directive would avoid many human tragedies resulting, for example, from the arbitrary and collective deprivation of thousands of officers and soldiers serving poland, even one day before 31 july 1990, of their pension rights arising from their service, as well as of the benefits associated with taking up any other job after the end of their service. the national courts have recognised the absurdity and repressive nature of such a practice by referring questions to the cjeu or ruling in favour of the injured parties in breach of the national rule. however, it seems that until a directive is adopted prohibiting discrimination on any ground, the national practice of applying blind collective liability without proof of fault will remain outside the scope of eu law.

member of the commission. – madam president, as stated already at the beginning of this debate, saving lives has always been, and will continue to be, the commission’s priority. it’s our moral duty and legal obligation to save lives at sea and grant protection to those fleeing persecution and serious harm, including as a result of war or conflict. to this end we have to continue building a wider, comprehensive strategy aimed at effectively managing migration in all its aspects. in parallel, we should continue our efforts to address the root causes of irregular migration and instability in the countries of origin and transit. we have to fight everywhere smuggling networks that ruthlessly exploit the vulnerabilities of desperate people. we have to offer more accessible and credible legal pathways of economic migration and resettlement for migrants and asylum seekers stuck in third countries. implementing this comprehensive strategy represents a very challenging task, which the eu should not address alone. the only way to achieve results is to continue working in partnership with countries of origin, transit and destination, with the support of international organisations and hand in hand with civil society organisations, sharing responsibilities in a true spirit of international cooperation. i am sure that all these elements will be reflected in the new pact on migration and asylum that the president-elect, ms ursula von der leyen, will present to give a new impetus to the european union response to migratory challenges.

on behalf of the ppe group. - madam president! - i have to go. the united nations convention on the rights of the child has profoundly changed the way our societies view children as the true rights holders. the convention has helped to both highlight the exceptional importance of children's rights and to ensure that member states and their governments recognise their responsibilities in this area. knowing full well that children's rights are human rights, we have a special obligation. we have a duty to promote and protect the rights of the child, both in our internal and external policies. first, children have the right to a childhood, to develop physically and mentally in a safe and healthy environment. they have the right to education and services that will help them become independent, happy and healthy adults. children have a right to a family life. finally, they have the right to be protected against all forms of violence, discrimination and exploitation. as we approach the 30th anniversary of the convention and appreciate all the progress made towards upholding these rights, it is also time to reflect on what has not yet been achieved. according to eurostat, children are still the age group most at risk of poverty or social exclusion. violence against children remains a real threat, both offline and online, in both social and family environments. more needs to be done to ensure that court systems address the specific needs and interests of children in their dealings with the law, and that they are subject-based rather than subject-matter. finally, as parliamentarians, we have a duty to our citizens, especially the youngest, to cooperate with the commission and the council, as well as with international organisations and with children themselves, because the voice of children should be heard.

in writing. our goals, as set out in the paris agreement, must be more visible to the people of our cities. investing in energy efficiency and reducing greenhouse gas emissions is important, but it is up to each and every person in the union to improve and deliver on our commitments. if humans understand the nature of climate catastrophe, the effects will occur at a much faster rate. so investing in green road infrastructure, funding electric cars, green start-ups are all actions that bring education and awareness. if we use green public transport every day, if we charge our green cars at green stations, the result will be to turn people into green, environmentally conscious citizens of the european union.
in writing. climate change is a global challenge. europe is taking a leading role in combating climate change and is committed to advancing progress towards a low-carbon economy to meet the goals of the paris agreement. to this end, the eu has developed a long-term strategy to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by finding the right policy mix between ambition and competitiveness of our companies. in addition, aircraft, new cars and trucks will be subject in the near future to stricter emission limits. energy is one of the basic elements of the european economy. our aim is to ensure a stable and sustainable supply at a reasonable cost to businesses and households. at the same time, the eu faces the serious challenges of energy import dependence and high energy costs, which are damaging the competitiveness of our industries in the global economy. we believe that the future lies in the energy union.
in writing. the cop25 climate conference is the first event where the new european parliament can express its opinion on an important global issue. it is also an opportunity to advocate for responsible action that addresses the complexity of the challenge, rather than simply raising awareness. a parliament resolution that prioritises a fair and competitive transition is therefore needed. all technological solutions are needed to simultaneously tackle the climate challenge, ensure stable consumer energy prices and avoid jeopardising the competitiveness of member states. these include nuclear energy, which is essential for the countries of the central european region to produce electricity in a cheap, emission-free and safe manner. without the involvement of additional nuclear power, the transition will be much more difficult, expensive and dangerous. so by demonizing nuclear power, you're making it impossible to take successful action on climate change, which is unacceptable to me.

the rapporteur. mr president, mr commissioner, colleagues, i would like to thank you for your support. let me begin by welcoming commissioner hogan, who is here as commissioner for agriculture, but as commissioner for international trade he will soon have a lot to do, i think, with ukraine and ukrainian free trade issues. fellow members, today we're going to talk about weird chicken and a legal joke. i thank the presidency of the european parliament for finally putting this subject on the agenda of the plenary. it has lessons that make me think that this is really the place for it. what exactly is this, the batman chicken? the eu-ukraine free trade agreement concluded in 2016 allows the import of ukrainian breast feathers under strict restrictions. there's a quota and there's a heavy duty on top. yes, but there are two other tariff lines in this agreement that are not subject to a quantitative limit, the tariff. at the time, the commission thought, in my opinion, that it was not a problem, that it was such a small quantity. yes, they did, but on the ukrainian side, some very clever, very shrewd people took advantage of that opportunity and used a lot of creativity to circumvent the free trade agreement. the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the commission's proposal is implemented in the appropriate way. the commission has also found that the measures in question are not compatible with the internal market. the commission has taken steps to negotiate with ukraine, through an exchange of letters, a solution which would bring trade back under the normal regulatory procedure by adding the two tariff lines concerned to the deregulated quota for breast-fillets and increasing the quota by 50 000 tonnes. i would also like to emphasise that the health and animal health standards were not called into question, so the union market was not threatened in this respect. in ukraine, i can tell you that the government has already approved this amendment to the agreement, and it was submitted to the parliament on november 15th. the relevant committees have already discussed it and we expect the rada plenary to put it on the agenda as soon as possible. finally, i would like to make a few requests. first, i would ask the ukrainian parliament to hold the debate as soon as possible and to contribute to the agreement. i also ask ukraine, which is an important geostrategic partner for us, we want to trade fairly with them, to act in the future according to the spirit and letter of the agreements, to apply them in good faith, not to exploit any loopholes, legal loopholes. finally, i would ask the commission to ensure that the next free trade agreements do not create a legal loophole which would allow them to be applied in bad faith. i think the commission has found a good solution, ladies and gentlemen, and i ask you to vote in favour of amending the agreement with ukraine, so that we can protect the market and our own producers.
member of the commission. – mr president, i wish to thank the rapporteur, ms győri, and the shadow rapporteurs for their speedy work on this report, and i welcome the clear decision by the members of the committee on international trade (inta) to recommend that the european parliament gives its consent to this agreement reached between the commission and ukraine earlier this year. i am grateful too for the favourable opinion by the committee on agriculture and rural development (agri) and i want to acknowledge the work of the rapporteur mr kuźmiuk. by giving consent to this agreement, the european parliament is once again protecting the interests of our agricultural sector. once parliament has given its consent, the council will have to adopt a decision on the conclusion of the agreement. as i’m sure you are aware, indeed it has been outlined very well by ms győri, the ratification process by the ukrainian parliament is still pending, even though the ukrainian government agreed the agreement on 23 october last. we have been doing our best to encourage the ukrainian parliament to proceed quickly with the ratification and i hope that they will do so when parliament reassembles in ukraine next week. in view of this likelihood and given the continued urgency of this issue, we are encouraging the european parliament to give its consent this week so as to allow the completion of the ratification process from the european union side. you are all aware of the background, and this again has been outlined very well by ms győri and she has explained the sad and unsatisfactory history in relation to the poultry cuts issue. i want to assure ms győri that the european commission will have learned lessons from this trading experience. the rapid increase in imports of the poultry cut in question did raise significant concerns due to the risk of potentially unlimited duty free amounts of poultry meat coming into the european market, particularly breast meat. in order to address these concerns, the commission began consulting with the ukrainian authorities last year and the agreement was concluded earlier this year. the solution provides for the inclusion of two particular tariff lines and the existing tariff rate quotas (trq) for poultry meat products, and an increase in the size trq by 50 000 tons, otherwise we would have an unlimited amount of poultry meat coming into the european union in respect of breast meat. out-of-quota imports under the other two problematic other cuts tariff lines would be subject to the most favoured nation tariffs. under the agreement reached, ukraine is effectively accepting a limit to its exports of poultry meat into the eu, and while the increase of a quota by 50 000 tonnes is indeed substantial, it falls clearly below the current ukraine export capacity of poultry breast meat. this agreement responds to a situation which threatened to present an enormous challenge to our eu poultry producers and i know that in your respective committees you have stressed the importance of monitoring closely the implementation of this agreement, which we will do. not alone can i assure you on this point, but i also want to assure you that all of our free trade agreements (ftas) have been screened, that there are no further such loopholes relating to poultry lines involved in any previous agreements and we did not find any. we are committed fully to a continued close monitoring of the implementation of this and other ftas and also, as you are aware, we are appointing a chief technical officer in relation to trade implementation and enforcement in 2020. while i welcome your acknowledgment that the agreement reached addresses the particular loophole, i do appreciate the concerns that have been expressed at the extent of the increase in the trq. i would point out, however, that the situation in question was monitored and identified at an earlier stage precisely because of this monitoring of our ftas but nevertheless it is a substantial trq revision that has to be made in respect of this agreement. i am grateful for the opportunity to contribute to this debate, to outline the background and also the action that we were taking, and also to thank again the parliament for their anticipated consent to this agreement.

upgrade the european civil protection mechanism through resceu in order to deal with natural disasters efficiently and effectively. but we have only taken one first step. we need more and more. so it’s your responsibility, as the european parliament, to go beyond, as we have already done as the former commission. thank you so much for your support. it is a common achievement, but my sincere advice, through the last five years of experience, is that you have to go beyond the first step in the resceu field. otherwise, we will face a lot of problems because the new phenomena due to climate change is so complicated and complex. nobody can deal with this phenomena alone because it is so complicated. at the same time, many of you already insist on solidarity. yes, solidarity is the fundamental principle for our union and this is why, now, some rescue teams, through the eu civil protection mechanism, are running and are in action in albania in order to save lives. i’m really proud of these institutions because the european union can provide solidarity in very difficult circumstances. at the same time, i would like to take this opportunity to say more about our eu initiatives that will help us address the challenge over the years to come. first, disaster risk management is vital, in particular for our cohesion policy. local and regional authorities are the first to face the impact of disasters. investing in risk management is cost-effective; it prevents future losses and it contributes to sustainable development. over the period 2014-2020, cohesion policy is investing almost eur 2 billion in climate change adaptation and risk prevention. as i said, prevention is the main focus of our investment, with actions to improve the modelling of risk, early warning systems, the preparation of strategies and guidelines, etc. in this period we have also seen a large focus on green infrastructure to manage risks. furthermore, under the urban agenda for the european union, the partnership on climate adaptation coordinated by the city of genoa is implementing ten actions to anticipate climate change and take appropriate measures to prevent or minimise the damage it can cause to urban areas. the commission has also launched the european natural hazard scientific partnership, a network of scientific european institutions and international organisations that monitor natural hazards. they are ready 24/7 to support the european commission and our emergency response coordination centre. besides prevention, we also focus on preparedness with support for equipment, infrastructure and training of civil protection units. we offer flexibility in our programmes. programme amendments can be proposed and swiftly agreed to shift resources towards areas that are most in need. so, if changes need to be made, we can still do this within this funding period. the second point is that we are promoting initiatives to mitigate the impact of climate change on cultural heritage. that is in particular the case with the support of the horizon 2020 programme with climate action, mitigating the impacts of climate change and natural hazards on cultural heritage. at the initiative of the commission, 27 european countries agreed to work closely together to advance the digitisation of europe’s cultural heritage in a declaration of cooperation launched in april 2019. the commission has also been funding the use of digital technologies for the preservation and restoration of cultural heritage. the latest initiative includes a future european competence centre for the preservation and conservation of european cultural heritage by using ict technologies, under horizon 2020 once again. the intersection between cultural heritage and climate change has also been under the spotlight during the european year of cultural heritage 2018 with the report ‘safeguarding cultural heritage from natural and man-made disasters’. in the same vein, the european framework for action on cultural heritage includes a focus on protecting cultural heritage against natural disasters and climate change. in 2021, a group of experts from eu member states will analyse and share innovative policy measures for heritage sites to mitigate the impact of climate change. with the support, of course, of horizon 2020, the commission is investing some eur 18 million in this field. so the list of what the european union is doing to protect our communities against the disastrous impact of natural disasters, but also to preserve our cultural heritage, is long. no doubt much more remains to be done. i know and am sure that we can count on your support and your initiatives in order to be more effective and more efficient. thank you so much for your attention and for this very constructive discussion.

election that took place last month. the european commission strongly condemns these developments. any form of discrimination, intolerance or violence based on sexual orientation, gender identity or sex characteristics, goes against the fundamental values of the european union that are founded in article ii of the treaty. in addition, article 21 of the charter of fundamental rights of the european union, which has the same legal values as the treaties, prohibits any discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation and sex. some of the polish authorities that have adopted anti-lgbti resolutions, declarations or statements, are managing authorities or beneficiaries of operational programmes supported by the eu structural and investment funds, and on 23 october this year, the commission met with polish authorities in the framework of an annual review meeting of the regional operational programmes that are financed or co-financed by the european regional development fund and the european social fund and we stressed the need to respect eu law, including the charter, in the implementation of these programmes, particularly the principle of non-discrimination. by issuing anti-lgbti resolutions, declarations or statements, polish managing authorities and beneficiaries of the eu structural investment funds raise doubts of their ability to ensure respect of the charter. the commission will continue to monitor the situation in poland, and we will engage with poland to make sure incidents of this kind never happen again. discrimination, violence and hate speech against the lgbti community must be stopped in the european union. thank you very much for this possibility to have the debate. i’m looking forward to your questions.

executive vice-president of the commission. – mr president, honourable members, i’ve listened very carefully to this debate and i’m really excited by the fact that this parliament has expressed such broad support for the european green deal. this is a great start of what is going to be quite a bumpy road, where we will need both institutions to concentrate on all the elements that we need to make the green deal work. first of all, let me say here today that i want to congratulate greta thunberg for having been nominated person of the year by time magazine. i think this is a great sign that this generation – our kids – are leading the way, and as a parent, there’s nothing more beautiful than when you see that your kids are leading the way. but that’s not the only reason why i believe we need to act now. the reason i believe we need to act now is because the facts are staring us in the face, and i think if you are a responsible member of parliament, if you’re in the responsible position in the commission, if you’re a citizen, if you’re a parent, you do not have the luxury to ignore the facts. look at what’s happening in greenland. look at what’s happening globally with our climate. look at the desertification. look at the erratic weather. look at the people suffering because of this erratic weather across europe. look at what’s happening to our biodiversity as we speak. we do not have the luxury to ignore this any more. and look at another thing that’s happening. we are in the middle of the fourth industrial revolution. that is going to change our economy, our industry, whether we like it or not, whether we act or not. so the question we have to face today as europeans is this: are we going to try and be masters of this momentous change, of this paradigm shift, or are we just going to let it happen, and then others will be the masters of it and we can just be the subjects of what others will decide? this is the fundamental question we have to answer, and the green deal is not a blueprint. it’s a roadmap. it’s an extended open hand to you and to all the stakeholders, whether it’s businesses, whether it’s ngos, whether it’s trade unions, whether it’s citizens, whether it’s cities, whether it’s regions, to be part of a discussion of how we are going to reorganise our society in a just way so that it reflects the values we want to stand for. and we need to do this because mother earth is fed up with this behaviour. and you know, she was able to exist for millennia without human beings; she will be able to exist for other millennia without human beings. we’d better make sure we create an existence in balance with her so that we can continue to exist as human beings for millennia. and this is the responsibility we have before our kids. but let me make a point, because it was said often: this is costly. yes, but don’t forget what the cost is of not acting. we see it every day. it was also said we have to be sure we take the right decisions. yes, that is why every proposal the commission is going to put on the table will be assessed for impact. impact assessment will be an essential element of our analysis, but we will do this in a very, very speedy and comprehensive way. for instance. to determine exactly what the reduction by 2030 should be, from 50 to -55% – we want to have an impact assessment on that. but we want to be ready with that impact assessment early in the summer next year, so that the european union is extremely well prepared, with a climate law for cop26 in glasgow, so that we can lead the way. i bring back a message from madrid – the cop, where i’m going to go back and present the green deal tomorrow. the message is this: we need european leadership. the message is also this: some of us are insecure about what we should do. but if europe leads, we might go in the same direction. i had meetings with ministers from many countries saying: climate neutrality by 2050 is a good idea, we might do things the same way. with the chinese we are in a debate. are we going to have collective global leadership on this? yes or no? we need to work on that, because if we do it together, the impact will be much bigger. but at the end of the day it is very important that this parliament take this in hand and make sure that parliament has a leading role, together with the commission, to convince our member states and council to do the right thing. and if we begin by enshrining in law that by 2050 europe will be climate neutral, then we can take steps back until today and just chart the map that we need to get there, and then we will discuss the measures we will need to take, whether it’s on ets, whether it’s on emissions, whether it’s on taxation, whether it’s on all sorts of other measures to make our industry circular, to make sure that there are jobs in this new economy. but finally, i want to add one thing which is very, very important. you know, the biggest risk here i see is that those who are most vulnerable in climate change see themselves also as most vulnerable in the answer to climate change, so that they start resisting the green deal because they feel that they are vulnerable. and at the end of the day, if they resist the green deal and they stop it, they will be the first victims of the consequences of not doing the right thing. so that’s why – and this is a fundamental point – if this is not a social green deal, the green deal will not happen. if this is not a green deal where the most vulnerable regions in europe – coalmining regions and others – do not see solidarity from other parts of europe, it will not happen. so we need a level of solidarity with vulnerable individuals and vulnerable regions to make sure the green deal can be delivered for all our citizens. and let me end, because mr lange quoted ‘man on the moon’, so i obviously though of the famous moon speech by jfk, and let me just amend it slightly and end with that. we choose to go (to the moon in his case), we choose to go for climate neutrality in 2050 and do the other things, not because they are easy but because they are hard, because that goal will serve to organise and measure the best of our energies and skills, because that challenge is one that we are willing to accept, one we are unwilling to postpone and one which we intend to win. madam president, commissioner, madam rapporteur, all the member states share the problem of tax fraud in transactions through electronic commerce in the european union. the estimated loss of vat revenue from crossborder transactions is around eur 5 billion. vat fraud in the supply of services has also been found, although this is certainly more difficult to quantify. member states alone do not have the information necessary to ensure the correct and effective application of vat rules. the exchange of data is not always possible due to legal constraints, which makes administrative cooperation inefficient in order to combat tax fraud in electronic commerce. we need new tools to fight fraud in cross-border e-commerce transactions. information exchange, agile decision-making and simplification of the rule are crucial to combating fraud effectively. we therefore support the proposal to create a central electronic system for storing payment information and the obligation for member states to collect and transmit information from payment service providers. for this, it is necessary to simplify, it is necessary to harmonize the data collection process and its format. this will make us more effective and will help us to avoid payment providers being obliged to present the same information in a different format in each member state. this will undoubtedly be an effective tool for the fight against fraud and will be an efficient action that will allow payment service providers to save time and resources, removing barriers to further implementing a true digital single market. mrs. pereira, congratulations on this good work. we must keep moving.
madam president, we are talking about the tax that is a major revenue source for member states. therefore, the fight against vat fraud and vat losses is to strive to minimise the impact on state budgets. it is a fight for our governments to finance hospitals, schools or invest in a safe infrastructure. according to statistics, the vat gap in 2017 amounted to over 137 billion euros; that means more than around 260 euros per eu citizen were lost. while the differences across member states vary, a unilateral fight to fight tax fraud is not efficient – only a common set of actions can solve or minimise the problem. hence, i welcome the commission’s proposals on the files we are discussing: introducing requirements for payment service providers, and strengthening cooperation within the eu in order to combat vat fraud. at the same time, i want to stress two issues. the commission should evaluate if virtual currency platforms should also be covered by the legislation. also, in order to have more precise data on the vat gap, i call on the commission to develop a common statistical approach to quantify this phenomenon.
i'm not going to let you get away with this. the scale of vat fraud in the european union is enormous, and it is not clear how big it is. the cooperation of member states in combating fraud is simply necessary. the ecr group supports the commission and the council in the fight against vat fraud and evasion, particularly in the area of e-commerce. it seems necessary to design better laws, better tools so that we can create a situation where businesses that want to grow, or consumers who want to benefit from the market, are not harmed by this legislation. the challenge is also clarity in the protection and collection of personal data here, of course, cooperation with the european data protection supervisor is necessary. we should be able to get information on the dishonest seller based outside the country of consumption, and the money saved can be directed to other important areas of state activity, as in poland. in recent years, poland has been very successful in combating tax evasion, and we have been using the funds from this fight for social causes. it is therefore a matter of determination to combat the vat loophole effectively, which will bring glory to all the countries of the european union and bring order to the law.

our welfare, our well—being depends almost fully today on carbon and we are dependent on that. we’re addicted to that. so we need to get rid of that addiction and we need to make sure that we can turning things round. we’re saying this is where we need to be in 2050 and then we take steps back until today and then we can chart exactly what needs to be done until then. our proposal is not a
